nerdc_curriculum.authority: Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC)

learning_objectives: Apply all laws of indices to simplify algebraic and numerical expressions
Define logarithm as the inverse of indices and use four-figure log tables
Use laws of logarithms to evaluate complex expressions
Solve exponential equations using logarithms
Apply the change of base formula in problem solving
Solve real-life problems involving indices and logarithms
content: Laws of indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
Zero index: a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a
Negative index: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
Fractional index: aᵐ/ⁿ = ⁿ√(aᵐ)
Definition of logarithm: logₐN = x means aˣ = N
Common logarithm (base 10) and natural logarithm (base e ≈ 2.718)
Laws of logarithms: log(AB) = logA + logB, log(A/B) = logA − logB, log(Aⁿ) = n logA
Reading and using four-figure logarithm tables: characteristic and mantissa
Antilogarithm tables and their use in calculations
Change of base formula: logₐb = log b / log a
Solving exponential equations: e.g. 3^(2x+1) = 81
Real-life applications: compound interest A = P(1 + r)ⁿ, population growth, pH scale
activities: Use four-figure log tables to evaluate (23.5 × 0.042)^(1/3) step by step, showing characteristic and mantissa
Solve the equation 2^(x+1) = 5^(x-2) using logarithms and verify the solution
Research and present one real-life application of logarithms (e.g. Richter scale, decibels, compound interest)
exam_focus: WAEC frequently tests simplification of index expressions, evaluation using log tables, and finding antilog — always show table reading steps
JAMB tests laws of indices (fractional, negative), change of base formula, and solving exponential equations — multiple choice means one wrong step loses the mark
Common trap: log(A + B) ≠ logA + logB — students must not split sums inside logs

learning_objectives: Convert numbers from one base to another (binary, octal, denary, hexadecimal)
Perform addition, subtraction, multiplication and division in different bases
Solve problems involving number bases in real contexts
Identify place values in any given base
Express fractions in different bases
content: Place value in any base: e.g. in base 5, 234₅ = 2×5² + 3×5¹ + 4×5⁰
Conversion to base 10 (denary): repeated expansion
Conversion from base 10 to other bases: repeated division method
Conversion between non-denary bases via base 10
Binary (base 2): digits 0 and 1; used in computers
Octal (base 8): digits 0–7
Hexadecimal (base 16): digits 0–9 and A–F
Addition in other bases: carry rule (carry when reaching the base value)
Subtraction in other bases: borrow rule
Multiplication and division in other bases
Fractions in other bases: e.g. 0.1 in base 2 = ½ in base 10
Application of binary numbers in digital systems and computing
activities: Convert the number 347 (base 10) to base 2, base 5, and base 8, showing all division steps
Perform (1101₂ + 1011₂) and (43₅ × 12₅) with full working, checking by converting to base 10
Design a table comparing the same number in base 2, 5, 8 and 16 for numbers 1–20
exam_focus: WAEC tests conversion in all directions and arithmetic in bases 2, 5, 8 — always show the repeated division or expansion working
JAMB favours quick conversion and addition/subtraction in base 2 — practise binary arithmetic to speed
Common error: forgetting carry-over in addition (e.g. 1+1 in base 2 = 10₂, not 2)

learning_objectives: Define and identify surds, rational and irrational numbers
Simplify surds by reducing the radicand
Perform the four operations on surds
Rationalize the denominator of surds
Solve equations involving surds
content: Definition: a surd is an irrational root that cannot be simplified to a rational number; e.g. √2, √3, ³√5
Rational vs. irrational numbers: terminating/recurring decimals vs. non-terminating non-recurring
Simplifying surds: √12 = √(4×3) = 2√3
Addition and subtraction of like surds: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2
Multiplication of surds: √a × √b = √(ab); (√a)² = a
Division of surds: √a / √b = √(a/b)
Rationalizing monomial denominators: multiply numerator and denominator by the surd
Rationalizing binomial denominators: multiply by conjugate (a + √b) → conjugate is (a − √b)
Conjugate pairs: (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b
Square roots of surds: finding √(a + b√c) in the form p + q√c
Equations involving surds: isolate surd, then square both sides; check for extraneous solutions
Relationships between surds and indices: √a = a^(1/2)
activities: Simplify (3√5 − 2√3)(3√5 + 2√3) and (1 + √2)³ without a calculator
Rationalize 7/(2 + √3) and express in the form a + b√3
Investigate: which of √2, √3, √4, √5, √6, √7, √8, √9 are surds? Justify your answer
exam_focus: WAEC regularly asks for rationalization of denominators with binomial surds — practise conjugate multiplication
JAMB tests simplification and multiplication of surds quickly; know √2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732, √5 ≈ 2.236
Trap: students square before isolating the surd, introducing errors — always isolate first then square both sides

learning_objectives: Define a polynomial and identify its degree and coefficients
Add, subtract, multiply and divide polynomials
State and apply the Remainder Theorem to find remainders
State and apply the Factor Theorem to factorise polynomials
Solve cubic equations using the Factor Theorem
Apply polynomial operations to real-world problems
content: Definition of polynomial: P(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁x + a₀; degree, coefficients, constant term
Operations on polynomials: addition, subtraction, multiplication
Long division of polynomials: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder
Remainder Theorem: when P(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder = P(a)
Factor Theorem: (x − a) is a factor of P(x) if and only if P(a) = 0
Rational Root Theorem: possible rational roots are ±(factors of constant) / (factors of leading coefficient)
Factorising cubic polynomials: find one root by inspection/trial, then divide, then factorise quadratic
Solving polynomial equations: equate to zero, factorise, apply zero product property
Sum and product of roots: for ax² + bx + c = 0, α+β = −b/a, αβ = c/a
Expanding products of three linear factors
Partial fractions: decomposing rational expressions into simpler fractions
Applications: projectile paths, volume and area problems modelled by polynomials
activities: Find the value of k if (x − 2) is a factor of kx³ − 3x² + 2kx − 4, then fully factorise the polynomial
Divide P(x) = 2x³ + 3x² − 8x + 3 by (x + 3) using long division and verify using the Remainder Theorem
Solve 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6 = 0 completely using the Factor Theorem
exam_focus: WAEC tests all four operations, the Remainder Theorem, and full factorisation — show synthetic or long division working
JAMB tests quick evaluation using Remainder Theorem and identifying factors — P(a) = 0 test is fastest
Key: recognise that if P(1), P(−1), P(2), P(−2) etc. gives 0 you have found a factor — practise these quick checks

learning_objectives: Solve quadratic equations by factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula
Determine the nature of roots using the discriminant
Sketch the graph of a quadratic function and identify key features
Form quadratic equations given their roots
Solve problems involving maximum and minimum values of quadratic functions
content: Standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0)
Factorisation method: find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b
Completing the square: ax² + bx = a(x + b/2a)² − b²/4a
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a
Discriminant: Δ = b²−4ac; Δ>0 two real distinct roots; Δ=0 equal roots; Δ<0 no real roots
Sum of roots α+β = −b/a; product of roots αβ = c/a
Forming quadratic from roots: x² − (α+β)x + αβ = 0
Vertex of parabola: (−b/2a, f(−b/2a)); axis of symmetry x = −b/2a
Direction of parabola: opens up if a>0, down if a<0
Sketching: find x-intercepts, y-intercept, vertex; plot and connect
Maximum/minimum value: vertex gives max (a<0) or min (a>0) of f(x)
Application: projectile motion, area problems, profit/revenue maximisation
activities: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by all three methods (factorisation, completing the square, quadratic formula) and compare working
Sketch the graph of y = −x² + 4x + 5, clearly labelling roots, vertex, axis of symmetry and y-intercept
A farmer encloses a rectangular field with 100 m of fencing. Find the maximum area using quadratic methods
exam_focus: WAEC requires all three solution methods — factorisation scores highest marks and shows understanding; completing the square is often specifically requested
JAMB tests discriminant conditions, forming equations from roots, and vertex/maximum questions
Avoid: dividing through by x (loses a root x = 0) and sign errors when applying the quadratic formula

learning_objectives: Solve two simultaneous linear equations by substitution and elimination
Solve a linear-quadratic pair of simultaneous equations
Interpret simultaneous equations graphically as intersection points
Solve word problems leading to simultaneous equations
content: Simultaneous linear equations: two unknowns, two equations
Elimination method: multiply equations to make one coefficient equal, then subtract or add
Substitution method: express one variable in terms of the other
Graphical method: plot both lines; intersection is the solution
Three equations, three unknowns: extension using matrices or Gaussian elimination (JAMB)
Linear-quadratic systems: substitute linear into quadratic to get a quadratic equation
Geometric interpretation: a line and a parabola can intersect in 0, 1 or 2 points
Discriminant tells the number of intersections: Δ>0 (2 pts), Δ=0 (tangent), Δ<0 (no intersection)
Word problems: formulate equations, solve, interpret solution in context
Age problems, mixture problems, distance-time problems modelled as simultaneous equations
Currency and trade problems common in WAEC contexts
Checking solutions: substitute back into BOTH original equations
activities: Solve the system: y = x² − 3x + 2 and y = 2x − 4, then sketch both curves and mark the intersection(s)
A market woman sells rice and beans. Rice costs ₦500/kg, beans ₦300/kg. She sells 20 kg total for ₦8,000. Find the kg of each
Two cars leave the same town in opposite directions. One travels 20 km/h faster. After 3 hours they are 300 km apart. Find both speeds
exam_focus: WAEC tests linear-linear and linear-quadratic pairs; show substitution steps fully for method marks
JAMB often disguises simultaneous equations in word problems — identify the two variables and form equations first
Check: always substitute both values back into original equations to verify — one mark may be awarded just for checking

learning_objectives: State and apply all standard circle theorems
Prove selected circle theorems
Apply circle theorems to solve problems involving angles in circles
Identify and use properties of tangents to circles
Solve problems involving two or more circle theorems
content: Circle vocabulary: centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc (major/minor), sector, segment, tangent, secant
Theorem 1: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc)
Theorem 2: Angles in the same segment are equal
Theorem 3: Angle in a semicircle = 90°
Theorem 4: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary (add to 180°)
Theorem 5: Exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral = interior opposite angle
Theorem 6: Tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Theorem 7: Two tangents from an external point are equal in length
Theorem 8: Angle in alternate segment (tangent-chord angle = angle in alternate segment)
Intersecting chords: PA × PB = PC × PD (chords intersecting inside)
Intersecting secants: PA × PB = PC × PD (secants from external point)
Constructing circle theorems problems: identifying the arc being used is key
activities: Draw a circle, mark a chord, and measure the angle subtended at the centre and at the circumference — verify the 2:1 ratio
Prove that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180° using the inscribed angle theorem
Solve a multi-step problem: given a tangent from external point P touching circle at T, with a chord through the circle, find multiple unknown angles
exam_focus: WAEC almost always has 2–3 circle theorem questions; identify which theorem applies before calculating — name the theorem in working
JAMB tests angle calculations from diagrams; the 'angle at centre is twice angle at circumference' theorem is tested most frequently
Trap: students confuse 'angle in same segment' with 'angle at centre' — always check whether the point is ON the circle or AT the centre

learning_objectives: Define and use the six trigonometric ratios for acute and obtuse angles
Apply the SOHCAHTOA rule to right-angled triangles
Apply the sine rule and cosine rule to non-right triangles
Calculate areas of triangles using trigonometry
Sketch and interpret graphs of sin, cos and tan
Solve simple trigonometric equations in given ranges
content: Trigonometric ratios for right-angled triangles: sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj
Reciprocal ratios: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ
CAST diagram: quadrant signs — All positive (1st), Sin positive (2nd), Tan positive (3rd), Cos positive (4th)
Special angles: sin 30°=½, cos 60°=½, tan 45°=1, sin 60°=√3/2, sin 90°=1
Sine Rule: a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC — use when given two angles or angle-side-side
Cosine Rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cosA — use when given three sides or two sides and included angle
Area of triangle: Area = ½ab sinC
Graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x: amplitude 1, period 360°; key points at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°
Graph of y = tan x: period 180°; asymptotes at 90° and 270°
Transformations: y = a sin(bx + c) + d — amplitude a, period 360°/b, phase shift, vertical shift
Solving trigonometric equations: find principal value, use CAST for all solutions in range
Angles of elevation and depression: bearing and surveying problems
activities: Measure the height of a building/tree on the school compound using a clinometer and the tangent ratio; compare with actual height
Sketch y = 2sin(3x) for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, identifying amplitude, period, maximum and minimum
Solve the triangle ABC where a = 7 cm, b = 10 cm, C = 50°, using both the cosine rule and area formula
exam_focus: WAEC tests sine/cosine rule, bearings, angles of elevation/depression, and graphs — show which rule you are using and why
JAMB tests CAST diagram for signs, solving equations in given ranges (e.g. 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°), and special angle values
Trap: using sine rule when cosine rule is needed (ambiguous case) — if given three sides, cosine rule; two sides + included angle, cosine rule

learning_objectives: Collect, classify and tabulate data in frequency distribution tables
Draw and interpret bar charts, histograms, frequency polygons and cumulative frequency curves
Calculate mean, median, mode and range for grouped and ungrouped data
Calculate variance and standard deviation
Interpret statistical graphs to draw conclusions
content: Types of data: primary vs. secondary; discrete vs. continuous; quantitative vs. qualitative
Frequency distribution table: class interval, tally, frequency, cumulative frequency
Class boundaries, class width, class midpoint
Bar chart: for discrete data; gaps between bars
Histogram: for continuous grouped data; no gaps; area represents frequency
Frequency polygon: join midpoints of tops of histogram bars
Cumulative frequency curve (ogive): plot cumulative frequencies against upper class boundaries
Mean for ungrouped data: x̄ = Σx/n; for grouped: x̄ = Σfx/Σf
Median: middle value (ungrouped); from ogive or L + ((n/2 − F)/f) × h (grouped)
Mode: most frequent value; modal class for grouped data
Variance: σ² = Σf(x − x̄)² / Σf; standard deviation σ = √variance
Quartiles, percentiles and inter-quartile range from ogive
activities: Collect ages or heights of 30 classmates, group into class intervals, and draw a histogram and cumulative frequency curve; estimate median and IQR
Calculate the mean, median, mode and standard deviation for: 12, 15, 18, 22, 14, 18, 20, 12, 25, 18
Read a cumulative frequency graph and estimate the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles
exam_focus: WAEC requires calculation of all four central tendency measures from grouped data — know the median formula for grouped data L + ((n/2−F)/f) × h
JAMB tests standard deviation, interpretation of histograms, and reading ogives
Trap: students use midpoints as raw values in ungrouped mean — ensure you use midpoint only for grouped calculations

learning_objectives: Define probability and express it as a fraction, decimal or percentage
Identify sample spaces, events and outcomes
Apply the addition rule for mutually exclusive events
Apply the multiplication rule for independent events
Calculate conditional probability
Use tree diagrams and Venn diagrams to solve probability problems
content: Definition: probability P(E) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of outcomes, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1
Complementary events: P(E') = 1 − P(E)
Sample space S: set of all possible outcomes
Event: any subset of the sample space
Mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) — cannot occur simultaneously
Non-mutually exclusive events: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) — one does not affect the other
Dependent events and conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
Tree diagrams: map all outcomes and multiply along branches
Venn diagrams for probability: regions represent sets; intersections represent common outcomes
Equally likely outcomes: fair coins, fair dice, well-shuffled cards
Permutations and combinations: nPr = n!/(n−r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!)
activities: Draw a sample space for throwing two dice; find P(sum = 7), P(sum > 9) and P(doubles)
Use a tree diagram for drawing two balls (without replacement) from a bag of 3 red and 4 blue balls; find P(both same colour)
Use a Venn diagram to show that 60 students take Maths, 45 take English, 25 take both; find probability of taking at least one subject
exam_focus: WAEC tests all rules — clearly state which rule you are applying; tree diagrams earn structured marks
JAMB tests combinations, permutations, and the addition/multiplication rules — know nCr formula
Common error: not distinguishing between 'with replacement' and 'without replacement' in dependent events

learning_objectives: Differentiate polynomial, trigonometric and exponential functions from first principles
Apply the product rule, quotient rule and chain rule
Find equations of tangents and normals to curves
Solve maximum and minimum problems using differentiation
Apply differentiation to kinematics (velocity and acceleration)
content: Concept of a limit: lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h = f'(x)
Differentiation from first principles for f(x) = xⁿ, yielding f'(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹
Standard results: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹; d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ; d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = −sin x
Sum/difference rule: d/dx[f(x) ± g(x)] = f'(x) ± g'(x)
Product rule: d/dx[uv] = u dv/dx + v du/dx
Quotient rule: d/dx[u/v] = (v du/dx − u dv/dx) / v²
Chain rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) × g'(x)
Second derivative f''(x): rate of change of f'(x); used to classify stationary points
Stationary points: set f'(x) = 0; maximum if f''(x) < 0, minimum if f''(x) > 0
Equation of tangent at (x₀, y₀): y − y₀ = f'(x₀)(x − x₀)
Equation of normal: slope is −1/f'(x₀)
Kinematics: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
activities: Differentiate f(x) = 3x⁴ − 2x³ + 5x − 7 from first principles for the x⁴ term, then use the rule for the rest
Find the coordinates of stationary points of y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 2 and classify them; sketch the curve
A particle moves so that s = 2t³ − 9t² + 12t. Find when the particle is momentarily at rest and its acceleration at those times
exam_focus: WAEC tests product/quotient/chain rules, stationary point classification, tangent/normal equations — always classify max/min using f''(x)
JAMB tests speed/velocity/acceleration problems and polynomial differentiation — know that velocity = ds/dt
Trap: students find stationary points but forget to classify them as max or min — WAEC often deducts marks for incomplete classification

learning_objectives: Integrate polynomial functions using the reverse power rule
Apply integration to find areas under curves
Evaluate definite integrals
Apply integration to displacement, velocity and acceleration problems
Use integration to compute volumes of revolution (extension)
content: Integration as the reverse of differentiation: antiderivative
Indefinite integral: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1)
Constant of integration C: determined from initial/boundary conditions
Standard integrals: ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫cos x dx = sin x + C
Integration of polynomials: integrate term by term
Definite integral: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a); no constant of integration
Area under a curve: A = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx (when curve is above x-axis)
Area between two curves: A = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx
Negative area: when curve dips below x-axis, use |∫| or split the integral
Kinematics integration: s = ∫v dt, v = ∫a dt
Substitution method: let u = g(x), convert integral in terms of u
Volumes of revolution: V = π∫ₐᵇ y² dx (rotation about x-axis)
activities: Find ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx and use the result to compute the definite integral from x = 1 to x = 3
Find the area enclosed between y = x² and y = 4 − x², sketching the region first
A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4. Find the velocity and displacement after 3 seconds
exam_focus: WAEC tests indefinite integrals with constants, definite integrals, and area under curves — always include +C for indefinite integrals
JAMB tests kinematics integration and polynomial integration — practise integrating velocity to get displacement
Trap: forgetting to add +C in indefinite integrals loses marks; confusing order of limits in definite integrals gives wrong sign

learning_objectives: Identify and produce the 44 phonemes of British Received Pronunciation (RP) English
Distinguish between vowels (pure and diphthongs) and consonants
Apply correct word stress in polysyllabic words
Recognize and produce minimal pairs to distinguish phonemes
Transcribe words using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)
content: Phoneme: smallest unit of sound in a language that distinguishes meaning
20 vowel sounds: 12 pure (monophthongs) + 8 diphthongs
Pure vowels: /ɪ/ (bit), /iː/ (beat), /e/ (bet), /æ/ (bat), /ʌ/ (but), /ɑː/ (bar), /ɒ/ (bot), /ɔː/ (bought), /ʊ/ (book), /uː/ (boot), /ɜː/ (bird), /ə/ (about)
Diphthongs: /eɪ/ (day), /aɪ/ (my), /ɔɪ/ (boy), /əʊ/ (go), /aʊ/ (now), /ɪə/ (here), /eə/ (hair), /ʊə/ (pure)
24 consonant sounds: plosives /p, b, t, d, k, g/; fricatives /f, v, θ, ð, s, z, ʃ, ʒ, h/; affricates /tʃ, dʒ/; nasals /m, n, ŋ/; approximants /l, r, w, j/
Voiced vs. voiceless consonants: voiced uses vocal cord vibration (e.g. /v/ voiced, /f/ voiceless)
Minimal pairs: words differing by one sound — /bɪt/ (bit) vs. /pɪt/ (pit); /sɪt/ (sit) vs. /zɪt/ (zit)
Word stress: primary (ˈ) and secondary (ˌ) stress; noun vs. verb stress pairs (ˈrecord vs. reˈcord)
IPA transcription: representing speech sounds in standardized symbols
Elision, assimilation and liaison: connected speech processes
Nigerian English interference: confusion of /ɪ/ and /iː/; /ɒ/ and /ɔː/; adding vowels to consonant clusters
Intonation patterns: falling tone (statements, commands); rising tone (yes/no questions); rise-fall (surprise)
activities: Listen to a recorded text and transcribe 10 words using IPA symbols, then compare with a classmate's transcription
Practise 10 minimal pairs (e.g. ship/sheep, pool/pull, fan/van) in pairs: one student says the word, the other identifies which of the pair was said
Record yourself reading a paragraph and identify three words where your pronunciation differs from RP; explain the phonemic difference
exam_focus: WAEC Oral English section tests: identifying correct word stress, choosing the option with a different vowel sound, and phoneme identification from IPA symbols or descriptions
JAMB tests phonemes, rhymes, stress patterns and silent letters — learn the IPA chart and practise applying it to common WAEC/JAMB vocabulary
Trap: Nigerian mother-tongue interference often causes /ɪ/ (short) and /iː/ (long) confusion — know that 'ship' and 'sheep' are different vowel lengths

topics.topic: Spoken English — Conversation, Interview and Debate
learning_objectives: Demonstrate appropriate register and etiquette in formal conversations
Conduct and participate in structured interview sessions
Construct and deliver a debate argument with supporting evidence
Apply turn-taking, listening and response skills in group discussions
Use appropriate stress and intonation in formal spoken contexts
content: Register: informal (casual, slang) vs. formal (professional, academic) — context determines choice
Conversation conventions: greetings, topic introduction, turn-taking, topic change, closing
Telephonic conversation: opening, identifying oneself, stating purpose, message-taking, closing
Job interview: preparation (research, attire), responding to questions (STAR method), body language, questions to ask
Debate structure: proposition and opposition; first speaker introduces motion; subsequent speakers rebut; summary speaker
Argument construction: claim → evidence → reasoning → conclusion
Group discussion roles: chairperson, secretary, contributor, timekeeper
Formal speeches: vote of thanks, welcome address, valedictory speech — structure and language
Non-verbal communication: eye contact, posture, gestures
Paralinguistic features: volume, pace, pause, intonation for emphasis
Persuasive language: rhetorical questions, anaphora, rule of three
Critical listening: note-taking, identifying bias, evaluating evidence
activities: Role-play a job interview for a banking position: one student is the interviewer, another the applicant; class evaluates using a rubric
Hold a class debate: 'Social media has done more harm than good in Nigeria' — each side prepares 3 main arguments with evidence
Listen to a radio discussion on education, take notes, and present a 2-minute summary to the class
exam_focus: WAEC Oral section tests register appropriateness, conversation completion, and debate/discussion language — know formal connectives (however, furthermore, nevertheless)
JAMB tests formal vs. informal register identification and conversation appropriateness questions
Key tip: in debate questions, use signposting language ('Firstly…', 'My opponent claims… however…', 'In conclusion…') — examiners look for structure

topics.topic: Reading Comprehension Strategies and Vocabulary in Context
learning_objectives: Apply skimming and scanning techniques to locate information efficiently
Make inferences and draw conclusions from unseen passages
Determine meaning of unfamiliar words from context
Identify the main idea, supporting details and author's purpose
Analyse figurative language, tone and mood in passages
content: Skimming: reading quickly for general idea/main point without reading every word
Scanning: moving eyes rapidly to locate specific information (dates, names, figures)
Intensive reading: careful, detailed reading to understand every word and implication
Main idea vs. supporting details: topic sentence usually comes first or last in a paragraph
Inference: reading between the lines — using clues in the text to understand what is not stated directly
Context clues for vocabulary: definition clues, contrast clues, example clues, synonym clues
Figurative language: metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole, irony, allusion
Tone: author's attitude toward subject (formal, satirical, sympathetic, critical, humorous)
Mood: emotional atmosphere created in the reader (suspense, joy, melancholy)
Summary writing: identify main points, reduce to 1/3 of original length, use own words, avoid opinions
Point-Evidence-Explanation (PEE) method for comprehension answers
Types of passages tested: expository, narrative, descriptive, argumentative, dialogue
activities: Take an unseen newspaper editorial; skim for 2 minutes, then answer 5 main-idea questions before re-reading closely
Underline 5 unfamiliar words in a passage, guess meaning from context, then verify with a dictionary and discuss accuracy
Write a 100-word summary of a 300-word passage, then compare with a partner's — identify what was missed or wrongly included
exam_focus: WAEC comprehension carries high marks — answer in COMPLETE sentences; reference evidence from the passage; do NOT lift long phrases word-for-word
JAMB tests vocabulary-in-context options — the correct answer fits contextually, not just definitionally; eliminate options that change the meaning of the sentence
Strategy: answer questions in order but save the summary/précis for last; if one question stumps you, move on and return

topics.topic: Essay Writing — Narrative, Descriptive, Expository and Argumentative
learning_objectives: Distinguish between narrative, descriptive, expository and argumentative essay types
Plan and organise essays using outlines
Write coherent, well-structured essays of appropriate length
Use appropriate language features for each essay type
Edit and proofread essays for grammatical accuracy and style
content: Narrative essay: tells a story from personal experience; first-person perspective; past tense; chronological order; vivid detail
Descriptive essay: paints a picture with words; sensory details (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch); spatial organization
Expository essay: explains or informs; third-person; logical organization; facts and examples; formal language
Argumentative essay: takes a clear position; provides evidence and reasoning; acknowledges and rebuts counter-arguments; persuasive language
Essay structure: introduction (hook + background + thesis), body paragraphs (topic sentence + development + link), conclusion (restate thesis + summary + broader significance)
Paragraph development: PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link)
Coherence devices: transitional words (however, therefore, in addition, consequently)
Vocabulary range: avoid repetition; use synonyms, varied sentence structures, active voice
Letter writing: formal (complaint, application, official request) and informal (to a friend/relative)
Formal letter layout: sender's address, date, recipient's address, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), subject line, body, complimentary close, signature
Speech writing: address audience, use rhetorical devices, persuasive register
Report writing: headings, numbered sections, objective third-person language
activities: Write a 450-word narrative essay on 'The day I learned an important lesson', then swap with a partner for peer editing using a checklist
Write a formal letter to the Lagos State Ministry of Education requesting more science laboratories for your school
Convert a given argumentative essay from biased (one-sided) to balanced by adding a counter-argument paragraph
exam_focus: WAEC essay carries 50 marks — 10 for content, 10 for organisation, 10 for expression, 10 for mechanical accuracy; examiners penalise heavily for off-topic, poor paragraphing and grammatical errors
JAMB tests formal letter format, essay type identification and register appropriateness in a multiple-choice format
Key: write AT LEAST 450 words for WAEC essay; start with an engaging first sentence; end with a definitive conclusion — do not leave the essay hanging

topics.topic: Parts of Speech, Syntax and Sentence Structure
learning_objectives: Identify and use the eight parts of speech correctly
Construct grammatically correct simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences
Apply correct subject-verb agreement in all contexts
Use tense forms accurately in writing and speech
Identify and correct common grammatical errors
content: Parts of speech: noun (types: proper, common, abstract, collective, countable/uncountable), pronoun, verb (transitive/intransitive, auxiliary, modal), adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection
Phrases: noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase, prepositional phrase
Clauses: independent (main) clause vs. dependent (subordinate) clause
Sentence types by structure: simple (one main clause), compound (two main clauses joined by coordinating conjunction), complex (main + subordinate), compound-complex
Sentence types by purpose: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory
Subject-verb agreement rules: singular subject → singular verb; collective nouns (committee, team) take singular verb; 'neither…nor' and 'either…or' agree with nearer subject
Tenses: simple (present, past, future), continuous/progressive, perfect, perfect continuous — 12 tense forms
Active and passive voice: transformation and appropriate use
Direct and indirect (reported) speech: tense backshift, pronoun changes, time/place adverb changes
Concord errors common in Nigerian English: 'they was', 'he have', 'the news are'
Common grammatical errors: dangling modifiers, double negatives, misuse of 'whom'/'who'
Punctuation: comma splice, full stop, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, inverted commas
activities: Analyse and label every word in 5 complex sentences by part of speech and function
Rewrite 10 sentences with subject-verb agreement errors, explaining the rule applied
Convert 5 active sentences to passive and 5 passive to active, noting when passive is preferred (scientific writing)
exam_focus: WAEC tests concord, tense, active/passive, reported speech and punctuation — grammar section is 10% of total; learn the 'neither…nor' rule and collective nouns
JAMB tests every grammar area in multiple choice — know irregular verbs, preposition collocations (depend ON, good AT, interested IN)
Trap: Nigerian English 'they said I should come' is correct Nigerian idiom but NOT standard English — avoid in formal written contexts

topics.topic: Literary Devices and Appreciation of Poetry and Prose
learning_objectives: Identify and explain major literary devices in poems and prose extracts
Analyse themes, characterisation and setting in prescribed texts
Write critical appreciations of unseen poems
Compare literary texts on the basis of theme, style and language
Interpret figurative and symbolic language in literary contexts
content: Figures of speech: simile (explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'), metaphor (implicit comparison), personification, hyperbole, oxymoron, paradox, irony, pun, alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia
Narrative techniques: first-person vs. third-person narration; unreliable narrator; stream of consciousness
Plot structure: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, denouement/resolution
Characterisation: direct (narrator tells us) vs. indirect (shown through speech, action, others' reactions)
Theme: central idea or message; distinguish from subject (topic)
Setting: time and place; how it creates atmosphere and affects character
Conflict types: person vs. person, person vs. nature, person vs. self, person vs. society
Poetry elements: rhyme scheme (ABAB, AABB), metre, rhythm, stanza, line, refrain
Types of poetry: lyric, narrative, dramatic, epic, sonnet, ballad, free verse, ode
Tone and mood in poetry: how word choice and imagery create emotional effect
Symbolism and allegory: objects/characters representing abstract ideas
Critical appreciation framework: title, context, theme, language/style, tone, structure, overall effect
activities: Write a critical appreciation of an unseen poem using the framework: title–context–theme–language–tone–structure–effect
Identify and explain six literary devices in a given prose extract, quoting the text and explaining the effect of each
Compare two poems on the same theme (e.g. war, nature) in a structured essay: what they share and how they differ
exam_focus: WAEC tests unseen poetry appreciation and literary device identification; always QUOTE from the text and explain the EFFECT (not just identify the device)
JAMB tests recognition of literary terms and identification of devices — know at least 20 devices with examples
Trap: saying 'this metaphor makes the poem more interesting' is too vague — say 'the metaphor of the eagle for freedom creates a sense of limitless aspiration'

learning_objectives: Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities with examples
Resolve vectors into components and find resultant using graphical and analytical methods
Define and calculate displacement, velocity, acceleration and speed
Apply equations of uniformly accelerated motion (SUVAT)
Sketch and interpret velocity-time and displacement-time graphs
Solve projectile motion problems
content: Scalar quantities: magnitude only (distance, speed, mass, temperature, energy)
Vector quantities: magnitude AND direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum)
Vector addition: head-to-tail (triangle rule) and parallelogram rule
Resolution of vectors: Fx = F cosθ, Fy = F sinθ
Resultant vector: R = √(Fx² + Fy²), direction θ = tan⁻¹(Fy/Fx)
Definitions: distance (scalar), displacement (vector); speed = distance/time, velocity = displacement/time
Acceleration: a = (v − u)/t; deceleration is negative acceleration
SUVAT equations: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = (u+v)t/2
Displacement-time graph: gradient = velocity; flat line = stationary; curve = acceleration
Velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration; area under graph = displacement
Free fall: acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s² (9.8 m/s² more precisely)
Projectile motion: horizontal component constant; vertical component affected by gravity; range R = u²sin2θ/g; max height H = u²sin²θ/2g
activities: Experimentally determine g using a free-fall apparatus or a pendulum; compare with standard value
Draw velocity-time graphs for three motions: uniform velocity, uniform acceleration from rest, and deceleration to rest; calculate total displacement
Calculate the range and maximum height of a ball kicked at 20 m/s at 30° and 60° angles; compare results and explain why both give same range
exam_focus: WAEC tests SUVAT equations, graph interpretation and projectile motion — identify u, v, a, s, t before selecting an equation
JAMB tests vector resolution, resultant calculation and graph reading — know that area under v-t graph = displacement
Trap: confusing speed (scalar) with velocity (vector); using distance in displacement questions — read each question carefully for which quantity is asked

topics.topic: Newton's Laws of Motion, Momentum and Friction
learning_objectives: State and apply Newton's three laws of motion
Calculate momentum and apply the principle of conservation of momentum
Distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions
Define impulse and relate it to change in momentum
Analyse frictional forces and calculate coefficients of friction
content: Newton's 1st Law (Law of Inertia): a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external net force
Newton's 2nd Law: F = ma; net force is proportional to rate of change of momentum
Newton's 3rd Law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction (action-reaction pairs)
Momentum: p = mv; unit: kg m/s; vector quantity
Conservation of momentum: total momentum before = total momentum after (in closed system with no external force)
Elastic collision: kinetic energy conserved; objects bounce apart
Inelastic collision: kinetic energy not conserved; objects may stick together (perfectly inelastic)
Impulse: J = Ft = Δp = mv − mu; unit: N·s = kg·m/s
Impulse-momentum theorem: applied in crash safety (crumple zones, airbags lengthen time to increase safety)
Friction: static friction (fs ≤ μsN) resists motion; kinetic friction (fk = μkN) opposes motion
Coefficient of friction μ: dimensionless; μk < μs always
Friction applications: braking distance, walking, driving on wet roads
activities: Set up a trolley experiment on a friction-compensated runway; verify F = ma by varying force and measuring acceleration
Solve a collision problem: a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s collides with a stationary 3 kg ball; find velocities after elastic collision
Measure the coefficient of static friction between a wooden block and different surfaces (smooth wood, sandpaper, carpet)
exam_focus: WAEC tests all three Newton's laws, momentum conservation in collision problems, and impulse — draw before-and-after diagrams for collision problems
JAMB tests F = ma problems, friction calculations, and impulse-momentum — identify the system, direction of forces, and apply conservation correctly
Trap: forgetting direction in momentum problems (make one direction positive, stick to it) and confusing static with kinetic friction

learning_objectives: Define work, energy and power with correct SI units
Calculate work done by a constant force at an angle
Apply the work-energy theorem
State and apply the law of conservation of energy
Distinguish between elastic and inelastic potential energy
Calculate power and efficiency of machines
content: Work: W = Fs cosθ; unit: joule (J); only the component of force in direction of displacement does work
Work done against gravity: W = mgh (independent of path)
Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv²; unit: J
Gravitational potential energy: GPE = mgh; unit: J
Elastic potential energy: EPE = ½ke² (spring); k = spring constant (N/m), e = extension
Work-energy theorem: net work done on a body = change in kinetic energy; Wnet = ΔKE
Conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed; only transforms from one form to another
Conservation in mechanics: KE + GPE = constant (no friction); ½mv² + mgh = constant
Power: P = W/t = Fv; unit: watt (W) = J/s
Efficiency: η = (useful output energy / total input energy) × 100%; always ≤ 100%
Energy resources: renewable (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass) vs. non-renewable (fossil fuels, nuclear)
Energy transformations: electrical → light (bulb), chemical → kinetic (car engine), solar → electrical (panel)
activities: Calculate the minimum power needed to pump 1000 litres of water to a height of 15 m in 5 minutes
Release a ball from different heights on a ramp; measure speed at the bottom; verify KE = GPE using v² = 2gh
Analyse a hydroelectric dam system: identify energy transformations from reservoir to electrical output; calculate efficiency if 20% is lost to heat
exam_focus: WAEC tests energy conservation, power, efficiency, and W = Fs cosθ for inclined planes — always check if the angle is between force and displacement
JAMB tests quick calculation of KE, GPE, power and efficiency — memorise KE = ½mv² and P = W/t
Trap: using W = Fs without checking the angle; efficiency above 100% is impossible — re-check working if you get this

learning_objectives: Define and classify waves (transverse, longitudinal, progressive, stationary)
Identify and measure wave properties (amplitude, frequency, wavelength, period, speed)
Apply the wave equation v = fλ
Describe reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference of waves
Explain resonance and standing waves
content: Wave: a disturbance that transfers energy without transferring matter
Transverse waves: oscillation perpendicular to wave direction (light, water waves, electromagnetic waves)
Longitudinal waves: oscillation parallel to wave direction (sound, compression waves)
Wave properties: amplitude (A) — max displacement; period (T) — time for one complete oscillation; frequency (f) — oscillations per second (Hz); wavelength (λ) — distance between two adjacent crests
Wave equation: v = fλ = λ/T
Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (law of reflection applies to all waves)
Refraction: wave changes speed and direction when entering a new medium; frequency unchanged
Diffraction: spreading of waves around obstacles or through gaps; most prominent when gap ≈ wavelength
Interference: superposition of two waves; constructive (crests meet — amplitude doubles) and destructive (crest meets trough — amplitude cancels)
Standing (stationary) waves: produced by superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions
Nodes: points of zero displacement in standing wave; antinodes: points of maximum displacement
Resonance: when driving frequency = natural frequency, large amplitude vibrations occur
activities: Use a slinky spring to demonstrate both transverse and longitudinal waves; measure wavelength, count frequency, calculate speed
Set up a ripple tank experiment to observe reflection, refraction and diffraction of water waves
Demonstrate standing waves on a stretched string: find the fundamental frequency and first three harmonics by adjusting tension
exam_focus: WAEC tests wave calculations (v = fλ), properties identification, and descriptions of interference/diffraction — sketch diagrams for full marks
JAMB tests v = fλ substitutions, transverse vs. longitudinal classification, and standing waves (nodes/antinodes)
Trap: confusing period (T in seconds) with frequency (f in Hz); remember f = 1/T

learning_objectives: Explain the production and transmission of sound
Calculate speed of sound in different media and at different temperatures
Explain echoes, reverberation, loudness and pitch
Describe resonance in air columns and explain musical instruments
Explain the Doppler effect and its applications
content: Sound: longitudinal mechanical wave requiring a medium; cannot travel in vacuum
Speed of sound: ≈340 m/s in air at 0°C; faster in liquids and solids (denser medium → faster travel in elastic media)
Speed increases with temperature: v ≈ 331 + 0.6T m/s (T in °C)
Frequency range: infrasound (<20 Hz), audible (20–20,000 Hz), ultrasound (>20,000 Hz)
Pitch: related to frequency — higher frequency → higher pitch
Loudness: related to amplitude and intensity; measured in decibels (dB)
Quality/Timbre: determined by harmonics present — distinguishes instruments playing same note
Echo: reflection of sound from a hard surface; time delay > 0.1s for separate echo to be perceived
Reverberation: multiple rapid echoes causing prolonged sound; affects acoustics in buildings
Resonance in closed pipes: fundamental wavelength λ = 4L; open pipes: λ = 2L
Harmonics: closed pipe has only odd harmonics; open pipe has all harmonics
Doppler effect: apparent change in frequency when source or observer moves; ambulance siren pitch rises as it approaches and falls as it passes
activities: Calculate the depth of a well by shouting and timing the echo; compare with a measured value
Investigate resonance in a closed air column (resonance tube): find the resonant length and calculate speed of sound
Record the frequency of a tuning fork as it moves toward and away from a microphone to demonstrate the Doppler effect
exam_focus: WAEC tests echo calculations (distance = speed × time / 2), resonance in pipes, and speed-temperature relationship
JAMB tests sound properties, Doppler effect (conceptual), and speed of sound in different media
Trap: forgetting to halve time in echo problems (sound travels to object and back); confusing closed and open pipe harmonic relationships

topics.topic: Electric Circuits — Ohm's Law, Resistance and Power
learning_objectives: State and apply Ohm's Law to simple and complex circuits
Calculate equivalent resistance for series and parallel circuits
Apply Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws
Calculate electrical power and energy
Describe domestic electrical installations and safety devices
content: Electric current: I = Q/t; unit: ampere (A); flow of charge (electrons in conductors)
Potential difference (voltage): V = W/Q; unit: volt (V); energy per unit charge
Ohm's Law: V = IR (for ohmic conductors at constant temperature)
Resistance R: unit: ohm (Ω); R = ρL/A (resistivity equation)
Series circuits: I same throughout; V = V₁ + V₂ + …; R_total = R₁ + R₂ + …
Parallel circuits: V same across each branch; I = I₁ + I₂ + …; 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: sum of EMF in loop = sum of potential drops (ΣV = 0 around loop)
Kirchhoff's Current Law: sum of currents entering junction = sum leaving (ΣI_in = ΣI_out)
Internal resistance: E = I(R + r); terminal voltage = E − Ir
Electrical power: P = IV = I²R = V²/R; unit: watt (W)
Electrical energy: E = Pt = IVt; unit: joule (J) or kilowatt-hour (kWh)
Domestic wiring: live (brown), neutral (blue), earth (green/yellow); fuses, circuit breakers, residual current devices (RCDs)
activities: Build series and parallel circuits using resistors; measure V and I at different points; verify Ohm's law and calculate equivalent resistance
Solve a complex circuit with two batteries and three resistors using Kirchhoff's laws
Calculate monthly electricity cost for a home with a 100W bulb (8h/day), 2000W AC (4h/day), and 50W fan (12h/day) at ₦50/kWh
exam_focus: WAEC tests Ohm's law, series/parallel equivalent resistance, internal resistance and power calculations — draw circuit diagrams before solving
JAMB tests quick resistance combination, Kirchhoff's laws, and domestic safety — know the 2-resistor parallel formula: R = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂)
Trap: in parallel circuits, total resistance is LESS than the smallest individual resistance; if your answer is larger, recheck

learning_objectives: State Faraday's and Lenz's laws of electromagnetic induction
Describe how an AC generator and DC generator work
Explain how a transformer works and calculate turns ratio
Distinguish between AC and DC and describe AC wave characteristics
Explain energy losses in transformers and methods to reduce them
content: Electromagnetic induction: EMF is induced when flux through a conductor changes
Faraday's Law: induced EMF ∝ rate of change of magnetic flux; ε = −dΦ/dt
Lenz's Law: induced current opposes the change causing it (negative sign in Faraday's law)
Magnetic flux: Φ = BA cosθ; unit: weber (Wb)
AC generator: rotating coil in magnetic field; slip rings maintain continuous rotation; EMF = NBAω sin(ωt)
DC generator: same but uses commutator and brushes to produce unidirectional current
Transformer: changes AC voltage; uses mutual induction between primary and secondary coils
Turns ratio: Ns/Np = Vs/Vp = Ip/Is (for ideal transformer)
Step-up transformer: Ns > Np → Vs > Vp (used in power transmission to reduce current and I²R losses)
Step-down transformer: Ns < Np → Vs < Vp (used at homes to reduce voltage to safe levels)
Power loss in transmission: P_loss = I²R; reducing I (by increasing V) reduces losses
Transformer losses: eddy currents (reduced by laminating core), hysteresis, copper losses (I²R in windings), flux leakage
activities: Connect a coil to a galvanometer and move a bar magnet in and out; observe deflection and identify Faraday's and Lenz's laws
Build a simple transformer with two coils; measure primary and secondary voltages; verify the turns ratio
Calculate: a step-up transformer has 500 primary turns and 5000 secondary turns; if primary voltage is 240V and efficiency is 80%, find secondary voltage and power delivered
exam_focus: WAEC tests transformer turns ratio, AC generator components (slip rings vs. commutator), Lenz's law direction and energy losses
JAMB tests transformer calculations (Ns/Np = Vs/Vp), step-up vs. step-down identification, and Faraday's law conceptual questions
Trap: for ideal transformer only, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; when efficiency is given, power_out = efficiency × power_in — do not assume ideal unless stated

learning_objectives: Distinguish between temperature and heat
Describe methods of heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation)
Apply specific heat capacity and latent heat in calculations
State and apply Boyle's, Charles' and the combined gas law
Explain thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases
content: Temperature: degree of hotness; measure of average kinetic energy of particles; SI unit: kelvin (K); K = °C + 273
Heat: thermal energy transferred from hot to cold body; measured in joules
Specific heat capacity: Q = mcΔT; c = heat required per kg per °C; unit: J/(kg·K)
Latent heat: Q = mL; energy required to change state at constant temperature
Latent heat of fusion (Lf): solid → liquid (e.g. ice at 0°C, Lf = 336,000 J/kg)
Latent heat of vaporisation (Lv): liquid → gas (e.g. water at 100°C, Lv = 2,260,000 J/kg)
Conduction: heat transfer through direct particle collision; metals are good conductors
Convection: heat transfer by movement of fluid (liquid or gas) due to density differences
Radiation: heat transfer by electromagnetic (infrared) waves; no medium needed; dark/matt surfaces absorb/emit best
Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (at constant temperature); P ∝ 1/V
Charles' Law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (at constant pressure); V ∝ T (in Kelvin!)
Combined Gas Law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂; Ideal Gas Law: PV = nRT
activities: Measure the specific heat capacity of water by heating a known mass and recording temperature change; compare with textbook value 4200 J/(kg·K)
Demonstrate convection using potassium permanganate crystals in a beaker of water on a tripod: observe coloured water rising then falling
Investigate Boyle's Law using a syringe: seal the end, push the plunger in/out, measure volume at different forces, plot P vs. 1/V
exam_focus: WAEC tests Q = mcΔT, Q = mL, gas law calculations and heat transfer mode identification
JAMB tests gas law substitutions, Kelvin conversion, and thermal expansion — ALWAYS convert Celsius to Kelvin before using gas laws
Trap: using °C instead of K in gas laws gives wrong answers — conversion K = °C + 273 is non-negotiable

learning_objectives: Describe the structure of the atom and the nucleus
Identify the three types of nuclear radiation and their properties
Apply radioactive decay equations and calculate half-life
Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion
Assess the benefits and hazards of radioactivity
content: Atomic structure: nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in shells
Proton number (Z): number of protons; determines element
Nucleon number (A): total protons + neutrons; mass number
Nuclide notation: ᴬ_Z X
Isotopes: same proton number, different neutron number (e.g. ¹²C and ¹⁴C)
Alpha (α) radiation: ⁴He nucleus (2p + 2n); strongly ionising; stopped by paper; short range in air
Beta (β) radiation: high-speed electron from nucleus (neutron → proton + electron + antineutrino); penetrates paper; stopped by 3mm aluminium
Gamma (γ) radiation: electromagnetic wave from nucleus; least ionising; stopped by thick lead or concrete
Radioactive decay equation: conservation of mass number and proton number
Half-life (t½): time for activity/amount to halve; N = N₀(½)^(t/t½)
Nuclear fission: heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei + neutrons + energy (nuclear power stations; atomic bomb)
Nuclear fusion: light nuclei combine to form heavier nucleus + energy (sun's energy source; hydrogen bomb)
Hazards: ionisation damages cells/DNA, causes cancer; safe handling: distance, shielding, time limitation
Applications: carbon-14 dating, medical imaging (PET, gamma camera), cancer radiotherapy, sterilisation
activities: Calculate the amount of a 200g radioactive sample remaining after 3 half-lives (answer: 25g); repeat for 4 and 5 half-lives
Draw decay series for uranium-238 → lead-206, showing each alpha and beta emission
Debate: 'Nigeria should build nuclear power plants to solve its electricity crisis' — students research and present pros and cons
exam_focus: WAEC tests half-life calculations, decay equations (balancing A and Z), properties of α/β/γ, and nuclear fission vs. fusion
JAMB tests half-life, nuclide notation, penetrating ability of radiations, and isotope identification
Trap: in β decay, A stays the same but Z increases by 1 (neutron becomes proton); in α decay, A decreases by 4 and Z decreases by 2

topics.topic: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
learning_objectives: Describe the structure of an atom including subatomic particles
Explain electronic configuration and orbital notation
Describe periodic trends across periods and down groups
Relate the position of an element to its properties
Explain the significance of the periodic table in chemistry
content: Atomic structure: protons (positive, in nucleus), neutrons (neutral, in nucleus), electrons (negative, in shells)
Proton number (atomic number Z): defines the element; number of protons = number of electrons in neutral atom
Mass number A: protons + neutrons; relative atomic mass considers isotopes
Electronic configuration using shells: 2, 8, 8, 2... (e.g. Na: 2, 8, 1)
Orbital notation: s, p, d, f orbitals; Aufbau principle, Hund's rule, Pauli exclusion principle
Isotopes: same Z, different A; same chemical properties; different physical properties (density, mass)
Periodic table: arranged in order of increasing atomic number; periods (rows) and groups (columns)
Periods: elements across a period have same number of electron shells
Groups: elements in same group have same number of valence electrons → similar chemical properties
Periodic trends across a period (left to right): atomic radius decreases; ionisation energy increases; electronegativity increases; metallic character decreases
Periodic trends down a group: atomic radius increases; ionisation energy decreases; metallic character increases
Important groups: Group I (alkali metals), Group II (alkaline earth metals), Group VII (halogens), Group VIII/0 (noble gases)
activities: Write electron configurations for the first 20 elements and place them correctly on a blank periodic table
Explain why Na (Group I) is more reactive than Mg (Group II) using ionisation energy data
Compare properties of Group I elements (Li, Na, K, Rb): reactions with water, melting points, density trends
exam_focus: WAEC tests electronic configuration, periodic trends, isotopes and the significance of group/period position
JAMB tests quick electron configuration, trend identification (which element has highest/lowest ionisation energy), and isotope mass calculations
Trap: confusing period (rows — same number of shells) with group (columns — same number of valence electrons)

learning_objectives: Explain ionic, covalent and metallic bonding
Draw electron dot (Lewis) structures for ionic and covalent compounds
Describe properties of ionic, covalent and metallic substances
Explain hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces
Relate bond type to physical properties (melting point, conductivity, solubility)
content: Ionic bonding: transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal; electrostatic attraction between ions; forms giant ionic lattice
Ionic compound properties: high melting point; conducts electricity when molten or dissolved; hard and brittle
Covalent bonding: sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms
Types: single bond (1 shared pair), double bond (2 shared pairs), triple bond (3 shared pairs)
Covalent structures: simple molecular (H₂O, CO₂, NH₃ — low m.p., poor conductors) vs. giant covalent (diamond, SiO₂ — very high m.p.)
Dative (coordinate) covalent bond: both electrons donated by one atom (e.g. NH₃ → BF₃)
Metallic bonding: lattice of positive ions in sea of delocalized electrons; explains conductivity, malleability, high m.p.
Electronegativity and bond polarity: polar covalent bond (ΔEN 0.4–1.7); ionic bond (ΔEN > 1.7); non-polar (ΔEN < 0.4)
Hydrogen bonding: strong dipole-dipole interaction involving H bonded to N, O or F; explains anomalous properties of water
Van der Waals forces (London dispersion): temporary dipole interactions; increases with molecular size; explains alkane boiling points
Lewis (dot-and-cross) diagrams: show valence electrons; ensure each atom achieves noble gas configuration
VSEPR theory: electron pairs repel each other; used to predict molecular shape (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, pyramidal, bent)
activities: Draw Lewis structures for NaCl (ionic), CO₂, H₂O, NH₃ and CH₄ (covalent); predict molecular shapes using VSEPR
Compare melting points of NaCl, H₂O, CO₂ and diamond — relate to bond type and intermolecular forces
Investigate solubility: test NaCl, sugar, paraffin wax, iodine in water and in hexane; conclude 'like dissolves like'
exam_focus: WAEC tests Lewis diagrams, identification of bond types, dative bonds, and properties linked to structure
JAMB tests bond type identification from electronegativities, molecular shape from VSEPR, and hydrogen bonding explanation
Trap: students draw Lewis structures without checking the octet rule is satisfied for all atoms except hydrogen (which needs only 2 electrons)

learning_objectives: Define the mole and Avogadro's number
Calculate molar mass of compounds and convert between moles, mass and particles
Write and balance chemical equations
Apply stoichiometry to calculate masses, volumes and concentrations in reactions
Determine empirical and molecular formulae from data
content: Mole: the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number, NA)
Molar mass: mass of one mole of substance in g/mol; numerically equal to Ar or Mr
Conversions: n = m/M (n in mol, m in g, M in g/mol); n = N/NA (N = number of particles)
Balancing equations: conservation of mass (atoms of each element same on both sides); conservation of charge (for ionic equations)
Molar ratios: coefficients in balanced equation give molar ratio of reactants and products
Molar volume: 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³ at STP (0°C, 1 atm) or 24 dm³ at RTP (25°C, 1 atm)
Gas stoichiometry: n = V/22.4 at STP; Gay-Lussac's law for gas volume ratios
Concentration: C = n/V (mol/dm³ or mol/L); C = m/(M × V) directly
Limiting reagent: the reactant that is completely used up; determines product yield
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%
Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; found from mass/percentage composition
Molecular formula: actual number of atoms; MF = (EF)n where n = Mr(compound) / Mr(EF)
activities: Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ required to produce 11.2 dm³ of CO₂ at STP using the equation CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
From combustion data (0.3g compound gives 0.44g CO₂ and 0.18g H₂O), find the empirical formula
Perform a titration experiment: determine the concentration of NaOH using standard HCl solution; calculate n = CV at equivalence point
exam_focus: WAEC consistently tests molar mass calculations, balancing equations, stoichiometry and concentration calculations — show mole map working
JAMB tests empirical formula determination, limiting reagent identification, and gas volume calculations
Trap: not multiplying concentration by volume in litres (not cm³); 1 dm³ = 1 L = 1000 cm³ — convert before using C = n/V

learning_objectives: Explain the factors affecting rate of reaction using collision theory
Define dynamic equilibrium and apply Le Chatelier's principle
Calculate and interpret equilibrium constants Kc and Kp
Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions with energy profiles
Apply Hess's law to calculate enthalpy changes
content: Rate of reaction: change in concentration/volume/mass per unit time; units: mol/(dm³·s)
Collision theory: reaction occurs when particles collide with correct orientation and energy ≥ activation energy (Ea)
Factors affecting rate: concentration (more particles → more collisions), temperature (higher T → more particles have ≥ Ea), surface area, catalyst (lowers Ea), light
Dynamic equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate; concentrations constant; only in closed systems
Le Chatelier's Principle: if a stress is applied, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the stress
Effect of increasing concentration: shift toward side that uses the added substance
Effect of increasing pressure: shift toward side with fewer gas moles
Effect of increasing temperature: shift toward endothermic direction (uses heat)
Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^x / [reactants]^y (concentration terms, using stoichiometric powers)
Exothermic reaction: ΔH < 0; energy released to surroundings; products at lower energy than reactants
Endothermic reaction: ΔH > 0; energy absorbed from surroundings
Enthalpy change ΔH: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants)
Hess's Law: total enthalpy change is independent of the path taken; ΔH(route A) = ΔH(route B)
Bond enthalpy: energy to break/form one mole of a bond; ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)
activities: Investigate effect of concentration on rate: react marble chips with HCl at 0.5M, 1M and 2M; measure gas volume every 30 seconds
Apply Le Chatelier's principle to the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃): explain why 450°C and 200 atm are used industrially
Calculate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O using bond energies; compare with ΔH from Hess's law cycle
exam_focus: WAEC tests collision theory, Le Chatelier's principle (explain shift with reason), Hess's law and energy profile diagrams
JAMB tests Kc expressions, Le Chatelier effects on equilibrium, and exo/endothermic identification from ΔH sign
Trap: students shift equilibrium in the wrong direction when temperature increases — temperature increases always favour endothermic side

learning_objectives: Name and draw structures of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes using IUPAC nomenclature
Distinguish between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons
Describe and write equations for combustion, substitution and addition reactions
Explain isomerism in organic compounds
Describe industrial importance of crude oil and its fractions
content: Homologous series: a family of compounds with the same general formula, functional group and similar chemical properties; differ by -CH₂-
Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; single bonds only (saturated); general formula; methane, ethane, propane, butane…
Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ; one C=C double bond (unsaturated); ethene, propene, butene…
Alkynes: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; one C≡C triple bond; ethyne (acetylene), propyne…
IUPAC naming: identify longest chain (parent), number from nearest branch/functional group, name substituents
Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different structural arrangement (e.g. butane and methylpropane C₄H₁₀)
Combustion: complete (excess O₂) → CO₂ + H₂O; incomplete (limited O₂) → CO + H₂O or soot (C)
Substitution reactions of alkanes: with halogens in presence of UV light (free radical mechanism)
Addition reactions of alkenes: Br₂ (test for C=C — decolourises bromine water), H₂ (hydrogenation), H₂O (hydration → alcohols), HX (Markovnikov's rule)
Polymerisation: addition polymerisation from alkene monomers (polythene from ethene)
Crude oil fractionation: refinery gas, petrol/gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen — separated by boiling point
Cracking: breaking long-chain alkanes into shorter chains and alkenes; thermal or catalytic
activities: Draw and name all structural isomers of pentane (C₅H₁₂) and butene (C₄H₈)
Test a sample of paraffin (alkane) and ethene gas with bromine water — observe and explain the difference
Model the structure of methane (tetrahedral, 109.5°) and ethene (planar, 120°) using clay/toothpicks, relating shape to hybridisation
exam_focus: WAEC tests IUPAC naming, reaction types and equations, isomer drawing, and crude oil fractions
JAMB tests structure identification, combustion equations (balancing), bromine water test, and addition product prediction
Trap: drawing incorrect structures for isomers; forgetting that alkenes decolourise bromine water but alkanes do not (under normal light)

topics.topic: Functional Group Chemistry — Alcohols, Carboxylic Acids and Esters
learning_objectives: Name and draw structures of alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters
Describe chemical reactions of alcohols (oxidation, dehydration, esterification)
Write and explain esterification and saponification reactions
Describe properties and uses of each class of compounds
Explain condensation and addition polymerisation
content: Alcohols: -OH functional group; CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH; methanol, ethanol, propanol
Classification: primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) — based on how many carbons attached to C–OH
Ethanol reactions: combustion (fuel); oxidation by K₂Cr₂O₇ (ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid); dehydration with H₂SO₄ → ethene; fermentation (yeast, 37°C, anaerobic)
Carboxylic acids: -COOH group; ethanoic acid (vinegar); propanoic acid, butanoic acid
Carboxylic acid properties: weak acids; pH 3–6; react with metals, metal hydroxides, carbonates to give salts + CO₂
Esters: -COO- linkage; formed by reaction of carboxylic acid + alcohol with H₂SO₄ catalyst; named alkyl alkanoate
Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (reversible); uses: flavours, perfumes
Saponification: ester + NaOH → soap (sodium salt of fatty acid) + glycerol; basis of soap making
Fats and oils: esters of glycerol and long-chain fatty acids; saturated (solid, animal) vs. unsaturated (liquid, plant)
Soap: sodium/potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids; hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tail
Polymers: nylon (condensation polymerisation — amide bond, loses H₂O); PVC, polythene (addition from monomers)
Amino acids: bifunctional (-NH₂ and -COOH); proteins are polypeptide chains
activities: Prepare ethyl ethanoate in the lab: mix ethanol + glacial ethanoic acid + H₂SO₄, warm gently; identify product by smell
Test ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: observe colour change from orange to green; relate to oxidation to ethanal/ethanoic acid
Make a polymer model: link paper clips as monomers to represent addition polymerisation of ethene to polythene
exam_focus: WAEC tests esterification equation writing, functional group identification, alcohol classification, and soap chemistry
JAMB tests ester naming from acid + alcohol reactants, saponification, fermentation equation, and dehydration of alcohols
Trap: alcohol naming — the parent chain must include the C bearing the OH group; methanol has 1 carbon total, ethanol has 2

learning_objectives: Distinguish between electrolytic and electrochemical (voltaic) cells
Identify products at the electrodes in electrolysis of common electrolytes
Apply Faraday's laws of electrolysis in calculations
Explain the principles of a simple cell, Daniel cell and the lead-acid accumulator
Describe industrial applications of electrolysis
content: Electrolysis: decomposition of a compound by passing electricity through its molten or dissolved form
Electrolyte: ionic compound that conducts electricity when dissolved or molten
Electrodes: anode (+) — oxidation occurs; cathode (−) — reduction occurs
Electrolysis of dilute H₂SO₄: cathode → H₂ (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂); anode → O₂ (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻)
Electrolysis of concentrated NaCl (brine): cathode → H₂; anode → Cl₂; used industrially (chlor-alkali process)
Electrolysis of molten NaCl: cathode → Na metal; anode → Cl₂
Selective discharge: ions discharged preferentially based on position in electrochemical series
Faraday's 1st Law: mass deposited ∝ charge passed; Q = It
Faraday's 2nd Law: mass deposited ∝ 1/charge of ion (or M/z ratio)
Faraday's constant F = 96,500 C/mol; m = (MIt)/(zF)
Electroplating: thin layer of metal deposited on object using electrolysis; applications: silver-plating, chromium-plating, zinc-plating (galvanising)
Voltaic/Electrochemical cell: converts chemical energy to electrical energy; e.g. Daniel cell (Zn/ZnSO₄||CuSO₄/Cu)
EMF and electrode potential: standard hydrogen electrode as reference; electrochemical series
Lead-acid accumulator: rechargeable battery; Pb(−) and PbO₂(+) in H₂SO₄; 2V per cell; 6 cells = 12V car battery
activities: Electroplate a copper key with silver using a silver nitrate solution; weigh before and after; calculate charge used
Measure the EMF of a Daniel cell; reverse the electrodes and explain why current now flows in opposite direction
Calculate the mass of copper deposited if 2A flows for 30 minutes through CuSO₄ solution (M(Cu)=64, z=2)
exam_focus: WAEC tests electrode product identification, Faraday's law calculations, and electroplating — always show Q = It then m = MQ/zF working
JAMB tests selective discharge, brine electrolysis products, and EMF calculation from electrochemical series
Trap: confusing anode (+ electrode, oxidation) with cathode (− electrode, reduction) — OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain

learning_objectives: Describe the ultrastructure of plant and animal cells as seen under an electron microscope
State the functions of all major cell organelles
Distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Explain the levels of organization from cell to organism
Describe osmosis, diffusion and active transport across cell membranes
content: Cell theory: all organisms are made of cells; cells are the basic unit of life; cells arise from pre-existing cells
Cell membrane (plasma membrane): phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins; semi-permeable; controls entry/exit
Nucleus: contains DNA (genetic material); nucleolus produces rRNA; nuclear membrane (double); controls cell activities
Mitochondria: double-membrane; site of aerobic respiration; produces ATP; called 'powerhouse of the cell'
Chloroplast: in plant cells only; contains chlorophyll; site of photosynthesis; has grana and stroma
Endoplasmic reticulum: rough (ribosomes — protein synthesis) and smooth (lipid synthesis, detoxification)
Golgi apparatus: processes and packages proteins; forms lysosomes; secretion vesicles
Lysosomes: contain digestive enzymes; autolysis; digest old organelles and foreign particles
Vacuole: large central vacuole in plants (water storage, turgor pressure); small in animal cells
Cell wall: in plants only; cellulose; provides rigidity; fully permeable
Prokaryotic cells: no membrane-bound nucleus; no membrane-bound organelles; naked circular DNA; smaller ribosomes (70S)
Levels of organization: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Osmosis: movement of water through semi-permeable membrane from high to low water potential (hypotonic → hypertonic)
Diffusion: net movement of molecules from high to low concentration down concentration gradient; passive
Active transport: movement AGAINST concentration gradient; requires ATP and carrier proteins
activities: Prepare, stain and observe cheek cell (animal) and onion epidermis (plant) under microscope; draw and label both
Investigate osmosis: place potato cylinders in distilled water, 0.5M and 1M sucrose solutions; measure mass change after 30 minutes
Examine and draw electron micrographs of a mitochondrion and chloroplast; identify all labelled structures
exam_focus: WAEC practical requires drawing and labelling cells from microscope slides — use pencil, clear lines, no colouring, scale bar if asked
JAMB tests organelle-function matching, prokaryote vs. eukaryote differences, and osmosis/diffusion definitions
Trap: confusing osmosis (water only, through semi-permeable membrane) with diffusion (any substance, no membrane required)

learning_objectives: State Mendel's laws of inheritance
Solve monohybrid and dihybrid cross problems using Punnett squares
Explain sex determination and sex-linked inheritance
Distinguish between genotype and phenotype, dominance, recessiveness and codominance
Describe mutations and their causes
content: Mendel's Law of Segregation: alleles separate during gamete formation; each gamete receives one allele per gene locus
Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment: genes on different chromosomes sort independently during gamete formation
Terminology: gene, allele, locus, dominant, recessive, codominant, homozygous (pure breeding), heterozygous (hybrid)
Genotype vs. phenotype: genotype = genetic makeup (e.g. Bb); phenotype = observed characteristic (e.g. brown eyes)
Monohybrid cross: Punnett square for one gene pair; F1 from PP × pp = all Pp; F2 3:1 ratio
Test cross: unknown phenotype × homozygous recessive; 1:1 ratio = heterozygous; all dominant = homozygous
Dihybrid cross: two gene pairs; 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in F2
Sex determination in humans: XX (female), XY (male); Y chromosome carries SRY gene
Sex-linked traits: genes on X chromosome (haemophilia, colour blindness); more common in males (only one X)
Codominance: both alleles expressed simultaneously (e.g. ABO blood groups: IA and IB codominant; IO recessive)
Blood groups: genotypes IA IA or IA IO = group A; IB IB or IB IO = group B; IA IB = group AB; IO IO = group O
Mutation: permanent heritable change in DNA; gene mutation (base substitution, insertion, deletion) vs. chromosomal mutation
Down syndrome: trisomy 21 (chromosomal); sickle cell anaemia (gene mutation, base substitution in β-globin gene)
activities: Solve: a tall (TT) plant is crossed with a dwarf (tt) plant — show F1 and F2 using Punnett squares; find phenotypic ratios
Solve a sex-linked problem: a carrier female (XᴴX) marries a normal male (XᴴY) — find probability of haemophiliac son
Construct a class blood group survey; calculate allele frequencies and compare with Hardy-Weinberg expectation
exam_focus: WAEC tests Punnett squares, genotypic and phenotypic ratios, blood groups and sex-linked inheritance — always define symbols at the start
JAMB tests rapid recognition of cross ratios, blood group compatibility, and mutation types
Trap: students confuse genotypic ratio with phenotypic ratio — in a monohybrid F2, genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 but phenotypic ratio is 3:1

learning_objectives: Identify the six classes of food and their specific functions and sources
Describe the human digestive system and the digestion of each food class
Explain the role of enzymes in digestion
Describe absorption and assimilation of digested food
Identify nutritional deficiency diseases common in Nigeria
content: Six food classes: carbohydrates (energy; e.g. starch, glucose, cellulose), proteins (growth and repair; e.g. meat, beans), fats/lipids (energy store, insulation; oils, butter), vitamins (regulatory; A, B, C, D, E, K), minerals (structural and regulatory; Ca, Fe, I, Na), water (solvent, cooling, transport)
Carbohydrate digestion: salivary amylase (mouth) → maltose; pancreatic amylase → maltose; maltase (small intestine) → glucose
Protein digestion: pepsin (stomach, acid pH) → peptides; trypsin/chymotrypsin (pancreas) → peptides; peptidases (small intestine) → amino acids
Fat digestion: bile emulsifies fat → droplets; pancreatic lipase → fatty acids + glycerol
Alimentary canal: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) → large intestine → rectum → anus
Digestion in stomach: HCl creates pH 2; pepsin activated; churning (mechanical digestion)
Digestion in small intestine: bile from liver/gallbladder; pancreatic juice (amylase, lipase, trypsin); intestinal enzymes
Absorption: villi and microvilli increase surface area of small intestine; glucose and amino acids into blood; fatty acids and glycerol into lacteals (lymph)
Liver functions: produces bile, deaminates amino acids, stores glycogen, detoxifies, produces blood proteins
Nutritional deficiency diseases: kwashiorkor (protein), marasmus (protein+calories), scurvy (Vit C), rickets (Vit D/Ca), anaemia (Fe/Vit B12), night blindness (Vit A), goitre (iodine)
BMI: Body Mass Index = weight(kg) / height²(m²); underweight <18.5, normal 18.5–24.9, overweight 25–29.9, obese ≥30
Balanced diet: adequate proportions of all food classes; varies with age, sex, activity level
activities: Perform food tests: Benedict's test for reducing sugars, Biuret test for proteins, iodine test for starch, ethanol emulsion test for lipids
Dissect a model of the human digestive system or examine a labelled diagram; trace the path of a bread molecule from mouth to blood
Survey classmates' diets for one week; assess for deficiencies; design a balanced Nigerian diet using local foods
exam_focus: WAEC practical tests food tests and enzyme action experiments — know exact colour changes: Benedict's (blue → brick red), Biuret (blue → purple), iodine (yellow-brown → blue-black)
JAMB tests enzyme-organ matching, deficiency disease causes, and absorption routes (blood vs. lymph)
Trap: confusing mechanical digestion (physical breakdown by teeth and churning) with chemical digestion (enzymatic breakdown)

topics.topic: Ecology — Ecosystems, Food Webs and Population
