learning_objectives: Define key ecological terms (habitat, niche, population, community, ecosystem, biome)
Construct and interpret food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids
Explain energy flow and nutrient cycling in ecosystems
Describe factors affecting population size
Explain ecological balance, biodiversity and conservation
content: Habitat: place where an organism lives; niche: role of organism in ecosystem (what it eats, where it lives, when active)
Population: all individuals of one species in an area; community: all populations in an area; ecosystem: community + abiotic environment
Biotic factors: living components (predation, competition, parasitism, mutualism, commensalism)
Abiotic factors: non-living (temperature, light, humidity, pH, wind, soil type)
Food chain: unidirectional flow of energy (producer → primary consumer → secondary → tertiary consumer)
Food web: network of interconnected food chains in a community
Trophic levels: producers (autotrophs — plants), primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores/omnivores), decomposers
Energy flow: 10% rule — only ~10% of energy passed to next trophic level; rest lost as heat, excretion, respiration
Pyramid of numbers: number of organisms at each trophic level
Pyramid of energy: energy content at each level — always tapered upward
Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, sedimentation
Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium), nitrification, ammonification, denitrification
Population growth: biotic potential (r) vs. environmental resistance; logistic (S-curve) vs. exponential (J-curve) growth
Conservation: biodiversity hotspots in Nigeria (Okomu forest, Cross River NP); CITES, IUCN Red List; deforestation, desertification threats
activities: Survey the ecosystem of the school compound: identify producers, consumers and decomposers; draw a food web with at least 10 organisms
Model population growth with bean seeds as organisms: start with 10, double each 'generation', graph the J-curve, then add a carrying capacity to show S-curve
Debate: 'Logging in Cross River National Park should be permitted for economic development' — use ecological arguments
exam_focus: WAEC tests food web construction and interpretation, energy flow calculations (10% rule), and nutrient cycle diagrams
JAMB tests definitions, pyramid types, and population growth curve interpretation
Trap: pyramid of numbers is NOT always pyramid-shaped (parasites can invert it) — pyramid of ENERGY is always pyramidal

learning_objectives: Define trade and distinguish between home and foreign trade
Identify and explain all trade documents used in buying and selling
Explain trade terms (FOB, CIF, C&F) and their implications
Describe the channels of distribution from producer to consumer
Evaluate the roles of middlemen in trade
content: Trade: buying and selling of goods and services for profit; creates utility (form, place, time, possession)
Home (domestic) trade: within one country; retail (directly to consumer) and wholesale (to retailers in large quantities)
Foreign (international) trade: between countries; exports (sell abroad) and imports (buy from abroad)
Balance of trade: value of exports minus value of imports; favourable (surplus) or unfavourable (deficit)

Trade documents: enquiry (buyer asks for price information), quotation (seller's reply with prices/terms), order (buyer requests goods), invoice (seller's bill showing quantity, price, total), credit note (refund due to returns), debit note (additional charge), receipt (proof of payment), bill of lading (shipping document), warehouse warrant
Terms of trade: FOB (Free on Board — seller pays until goods on ship), CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight — seller pays all until destination port), C&F or CFR (Cost and Freight only, no insurance)
Trade terms for payment: prompt payment, cash on delivery (COD), credit terms (30/60/90 days)
Channels of distribution: manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer (traditional); direct selling; online
Wholesaler functions: buying in bulk, breaking bulk, storage, risk bearing, credit to retailers, market information
Retailer functions: final link to consumer, display, credit to customers, after-sales service, small quantities
Types of retail outlets: departmental stores, supermarkets, multiple shops (chain stores), cooperative shops, market stalls, kiosks
Elimination of middlemen: advantages (lower prices) and disadvantages (manufacturer takes on wholesaler/retailer functions)
activities: Trace the journey of a bag of rice from the Rice Farmers' Association in Benue to a Lagos market woman: identify each document exchanged at each stage
Collect and analyse real or sample trade documents (invoice, credit note, delivery note); identify all key information on each
Debate: 'Middlemen should be eliminated from the distribution chain in Nigeria' — argue both sides using real market examples
exam_focus: WAEC tests document identification, trade terms (FOB vs. CIF), channels of distribution, and functions of wholesalers/retailers
JAMB tests document purpose matching, balance of trade calculation, and retail outlet identification
Trap: confusing invoice (unpaid bill from seller) with receipt (proof of payment by buyer) — different documents, different timing

topics.topic: Aids to Trade — Banking, Insurance, Transport, Warehousing, Communication
learning_objectives: Identify the main aids to trade and explain how each facilitates commerce
Describe types of banks and banking services
Explain principles and types of insurance
Describe types of transport and their suitability for different goods
Explain the role of warehousing and communication in trade
content: Aids to trade: banking, insurance, transportation, warehousing, communication, advertising — they remove the barriers to trade
Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN): regulates banking sector; controls money supply; lender of last resort; issues currency; manages foreign exchange
Commercial banks: accept deposits; grant loans; operate current, savings and fixed deposit accounts; issue cheques
Services: current account (cheques, no interest), savings account (interest, limited withdrawals), fixed deposit (higher interest, fixed term)
Insurance: protection against financial loss in exchange for a premium; types: life, fire, marine, motor, employer's liability, accident, burglary
Principles of insurance: insurable interest, utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei), indemnity, subrogation, contribution, proximate cause, salvage

Transport: road (flexible, door-to-door, best for perishables), rail (heavy goods, long distance, reliable), air (fastest, expensive, perishables, valuables), sea/water (heavy/bulky goods, cheapest per ton, slow), pipeline (oil and gas only)
Warehousing: bonded warehouse (imported goods before duty paid), cold storage (perishables), general warehouse, private warehouse
Functions of warehouse: storage, bulk-breaking, blending, conditioning, financing (as security for loans)
Communication in trade: GSM, internet (e-commerce), postal services, radio/TV advertising
E-commerce: buying and selling online; platforms like Jumia, Konga in Nigeria; advantages (24/7, wide reach) and disadvantages (fraud risk, logistics)
activities: Visit (or simulate) a bank: identify services offered on a brochure; complete a sample deposit slip, withdrawal form and cheque
Role-play: an importer files a marine insurance claim after goods were damaged at sea — what principles apply and what documents are needed?
Compare the cost and time of sending 1 tonne of goods from Lagos to Kano by road, rail and air; recommend a mode for fresh tomatoes vs. iron rods
exam_focus: WAEC tests all 6 principles of insurance, types of bank accounts, modes of transport with their suitability, and warehouse types
JAMB tests CBN functions, insurance principle identification from scenarios, and transport mode matching
Trap: the principle of INDEMNITY does not apply to life insurance (you cannot be compensated for a life in monetary terms — life policies are valued, not indemnity policies)

learning_objectives: Identify and compare the main forms of business organization
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each form
Explain the process of forming a company (Memorandum, Articles of Association)
Distinguish between public and private limited companies
Explain the role of public enterprises in Nigeria
content: Sole proprietorship: owned and managed by one person; unlimited liability; easy to set up; all profit to owner; limited capital
Partnership: 2–20 persons (banking: 2–10); governed by Partnership Act; unlimited liability (unless limited partnership); Deed of Partnership
Limited liability company: separate legal entity; limited liability; can sue and be sued; minimum 2 directors
Private limited company (Ltd): shares not publicly traded; minimum 1 shareholder; maximum 50 (Companies Act Nigeria)
Public limited company (Plc): shares on stock exchange; wider ownership; more regulation; prospectus required
Formation documents: Memorandum of Association (objects, name, capital, liability — external); Articles of Association (internal rules — meetings, directors)
Cooperative society: owned and managed by members for mutual benefit; UNICOOP; retail, farming, thrift
Public enterprises (parastatals): owned by government; provide essential services; NNPC, NEPA/PHCN, NIPOST
Privatisation and commercialisation: government selling/commercialising parastatals for efficiency
Joint venture: two or more companies combining resources for a specific project
Franchise: franchise gives a franchisee right to use its brand and system (e.g. MTN franchises)
Multinational corporations (MNCs): operating in multiple countries; e.g. Shell, Unilever, Dangote
activities: Using the CAC (Corporate Affairs Commission) website, identify what documents are needed to register a business in Nigeria as a sole trader vs. a limited company
Case study: compare Dangote Group (Plc) and a local market trader (sole proprietor) on 5 criteria: capital, liability, control, continuity, regulation
Group activity: form a cooperative society in class — draft a simple constitution, elect officers, collect ₦50 dues per member, plan how to use the fund
exam_focus: WAEC tests comparing business forms on specific criteria (liability, management, capital), company formation documents, and public enterprise examples in Nigeria
JAMB tests definition-matching, Memorandum vs. Articles of Association distinction, and advantages/disadvantages identification
Trap: Memorandum of Association deals with EXTERNAL matters (name, objects, capital); Articles deals with INTERNAL management — students frequently reverse these

topics.topic: Accounting Concepts, Conventions and Double Entry
learning_objectives: Define accounting and state its objectives
Identify and explain key accounting concepts and conventions
Apply the double-entry principle to record business transactions
Distinguish between assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses
Prepare journal entries and post to ledger accounts
content: Accounting: systematic recording, classifying, summarising and communicating financial information
Purpose: decision making (management), taxation, reporting to investors, regulatory compliance

Accounting concepts: entity (business separate from owner), going concern (business will continue), accrual (record when earned/incurred not when cash received/paid), consistency (same methods year to year), prudence (caution; recognise losses immediately, profits only when certain), materiality (significant items only), matching (expenses matched to revenue they generate)
Accounting equation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities (or A = C + L)
Double-entry principle: every transaction has two equal and opposite effects; debit one account, credit another
Debit: increases assets and expenses; decreases liabilities, capital and income
Credit: increases liabilities, capital and income; decreases assets and expenses
DEAD CLIC rule: Debit = Expenses, Assets, Drawings; Credit = Liabilities, Income, Capital
Types of accounts: real (assets — physical), personal (debtors/creditors — persons), nominal (income/expenses — revenue)
Journal: book of original entry; records transactions chronologically with narration
Ledger: book of secondary entry; contains all accounts; grouped in sales, purchase, general ledger
Posting: transferring journal entries to the appropriate ledger accounts
activities: Record 10 transactions in a journal including purchases, sales, expenses and drawings; post to T-accounts in the ledger
Analyse: 'Owner puts ₦500,000 into business' — identify which accounts are affected; debit and credit sides
Class exercise: from a list of 20 accounts, classify each as asset, liability, capital, income or expense
exam_focus: WAEC tests journal entries, ledger posting, identification of debit/credit effects, and accounting concepts in scenario questions
JAMB tests DEAD CLIC rules, accounting concept identification, and the accounting equation
Trap: students debit and credit in reverse — use the DEAD CLIC rule consistently and practise until it is instinctive

topics.topic: Books of Original Entry — Subsidiary Books
learning_objectives: Identify and explain the function of each subsidiary book
Record credit transactions in the appropriate subsidiary book
Total and post subsidiary book totals to the ledger
Prepare a petty cash book using the imprest system
Balance and interpret a cash book with bank and cash columns
content: Subsidiary books (books of prime entry): Sales Day Book, Purchases Day Book, Sales Returns (Returns Inward) Book, Purchases Returns (Returns Outward) Book, Bills Receivable Book, Bills Payable Book, Journal Proper (for non-routine items), Cash Book
Sales Day Book: records all credit sales; columns for date, customer, invoice no., amount; total posted to Sales Account (Cr)
Purchases Day Book: records all credit purchases; total posted to Purchases Account (Dr)
Returns Inward Book: goods returned by customers; total posted to Returns Inward Account (Dr)
Returns Outward Book: goods returned to suppliers; total posted to Returns Outward Account (Cr)
Cash Book: records all receipts and payments in cash and/or bank; acts as both journal AND ledger for cash/bank
Two-column cash book: cash column and bank column; contra entries (C) when cash withdrawn from bank or deposited
Three-column cash book: adds discount allowed (Dr) and discount received (Cr) columns
Petty Cash Book: records small expenses; analysed columns (postage, stationery, sundries, etc.)
Imprest system: petty cashier given a fixed amount (float); reimbursed by the difference spent at end of period
Bank reconciliation: explains difference between cash book bank balance and bank statement balance; timing differences (unpresented cheques, uncredited deposits)
activities: Record a week's transactions in the appropriate subsidiary books; total each book and identify the ledger postings
Prepare a three-column cash book from a list of transactions and balance it at month-end
Given a cash book balance of ₦12,500 and a bank statement balance of ₦15,000 with two unpresented cheques (₦1,000 and ₦1,500) and one uncleared deposit (₦500), prepare a bank reconciliation statement
exam_focus: WAEC tests recording in the correct subsidiary book, cash book balancing with contra entries, and bank reconciliation
JAMB tests book identification from transaction type and imprest petty cash top-up calculation
Trap: forgetting contra entries in the cash book when cash is deposited to bank or withdrawn from bank — these appear on BOTH sides of the cash book

topics.topic: Trial Balance and Final Accounts of a Sole Trader
learning_objectives: Extract a trial balance from ledger accounts
Prepare a trading account to calculate gross profit
Prepare a profit and loss account to calculate net profit
Prepare a balance sheet to show financial position
Make adjustments for accruals, prepayments, depreciation and bad debts
content: Trial balance: list of all ledger account balances; debits = credits if correctly posted; detects arithmetic errors
Errors NOT detected by trial balance: errors of omission, commission, principle, compensating errors, reversal of entries
Trading Account: Sales − Cost of Goods Sold = Gross Profit; COGS = Opening Stock + Purchases − Returns Out − Closing Stock
Profit and Loss Account: Gross Profit + Other Income − Expenses = Net Profit (or Net Loss)
Balance Sheet: not an account; snapshot of financial position at a specific date; Assets = Capital + Liabilities
Current assets: cash, bank, debtors, stock, prepayments (expected to be converted to cash within 1 year)
Non-current (fixed) assets: land, buildings, machinery, motor vehicles (used for more than 1 year)
Current liabilities: creditors, bank overdraft, accruals, short-term loans (due within 1 year)
Non-current liabilities: long-term loans, mortgage (due after 1 year)
Capital section: opening capital + net profit − drawings = closing capital
Accruals: expenses incurred but not yet paid — add to expense in P&L, show as current liability in balance sheet
Prepayments: expenses paid in advance — deduct from expense in P&L, show as current asset in balance sheet

Depreciation: systematic reduction in value of fixed assets; straight-line (fixed amount each year), reducing balance (fixed percentage); charged as expense in P&L; reduces fixed asset in balance sheet
activities: From a given list of account balances, prepare a full set of final accounts (Trading A/c, P&L A/c, Balance Sheet) for a sole trader
Make adjustments: given accrued wages of ₦5,000, prepaid rent of ₦2,000, and a machine depreciated at 20% on cost, adjust the final accounts
Interpret a balance sheet: calculate current ratio, quick ratio, and working capital; comment on the business's liquidity
exam_focus: WAEC questions always include adjustments — memorise: accruals ADD to expense (P&L) and appear as creditor (Balance Sheet); prepayments DEDUCT from expense and appear as debtor
JAMB tests classification of items into correct balance sheet sections, gross profit calculation, and depreciation calculation
Trap: forgetting to carry closing stock into the balance sheet as a current asset after it has been used in the trading account

topics.topic: Introduction to Marketing and the Marketing Mix
learning_objectives: Define marketing and explain its core concepts
Distinguish between selling and marketing orientations
Identify and explain the 4Ps of the marketing mix
Explain market segmentation, targeting and positioning
Analyse how Nigerian businesses use the marketing mix
content: Marketing: the process of identifying, creating, communicating and delivering value to satisfy customer needs profitably
Core concepts: needs (basic human requirements), wants (needs shaped by culture/personality), demand (wants backed by purchasing power), product, value, exchange, market
Production orientation: focuses on making products efficiently; assumes demand exists
Sales orientation: focuses on aggressive selling to push products already made
Marketing orientation: focuses on customer needs FIRST, then producing what satisfies them
Societal marketing orientation: considers long-term societal welfare as well as customer satisfaction and profit
4Ps of marketing mix: Product, Price, Place, Promotion
Product: what is offered (goods, services, ideas); product levels (core benefit, tangible product, augmented product); product life cycle (introduction, growth, maturity, decline)
Price: amount paid; pricing strategies (penetration, skimming, competitive, cost-plus, psychological pricing)
Place (distribution): how product reaches customer; channels, logistics, wholesalers, retailers, e-commerce
Promotion: communicating with target market; advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling, direct marketing
Market segmentation: dividing market into distinct groups; bases: demographic (age, gender, income), geographic (region), psychographic (lifestyle), behavioural (usage rate)
Target market: the segment(s) the company decides to serve
Positioning: how customers perceive the product relative to competitors; positioning statement
activities: Analyse a popular Nigerian product (e.g. Indomie noodles, Bigi soft drink) using the 4Ps framework; present findings
Identify the market segment for three different products: luxury cars, sachet water, and university textbooks
Design a simple marketing plan for a new jollof rice restaurant in your school's neighbourhood
exam_focus: WAEC tests the 4Ps with specific examples, orientation types (production vs. marketing), and market segmentation bases
Common question: 'Give two elements of the marketing mix for a beverage company' — know Product, Price, Place and Promotion with Nigerian examples
Trap: confusing 'selling' (pushing what is made) with 'marketing' (making what customers want) — these represent different business philosophies

learning_objectives: Explain the consumer buying decision process
Identify factors that influence consumer behaviour
Define market research and describe its process
Distinguish between primary and secondary research methods
Interpret simple market research data
content: Consumer buying decision process: problem recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase decision → post-purchase evaluation
Cultural factors: culture, subculture, social class influence buying behaviour
Social factors: reference groups (family, friends, celebrities), social roles, status
Personal factors: age, occupation, income, lifestyle, personality
Psychological factors: motivation (Maslow's hierarchy of needs), perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes
Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → social/belonging → esteem → self-actualization
B2C (business to consumer) vs. B2B (business to business) buying decisions — B2B is more rational, formal, longer process
Market research: systematic gathering, recording and analysis of data about market, customers, and competition
Primary research: new data collected for specific purpose; surveys, interviews, observation, experiments, focus groups
Secondary research: existing data; government statistics, trade journals, company reports, internet databases
Survey methods: questionnaire (postal, online, personal interview), telephone surveys
Sampling: population vs. sample; random, stratified, quota, cluster sampling
Data analysis: frequency distribution, averages, graphs; qualitative vs. quantitative data
activities: Design a 10-question questionnaire to find out students' preference between three snack brands; conduct the survey and tabulate results
Role-play: a Lagos-based cosmetics company wants to launch a new product for young women; design the market research plan (objectives, method, sample, analysis)
Analyse a provided market research report; identify three key insights and suggest two marketing actions based on the findings
exam_focus: WAEC tests the five-step buying decision process, factors influencing consumer behaviour, and primary vs. secondary research distinction
Know Maslow's hierarchy by name and order — questions may ask which level is being addressed by a specific marketing appeal
Trap: 'secondary research' does not mean 'second-best' — it refers to data ALREADY collected; primary is NEW data you collect yourself

topics.topic: Product Development, Branding and Pricing Strategies
learning_objectives: Describe the product life cycle and marketing implications at each stage
Explain branding, packaging and labelling decisions
Distinguish between pricing strategies and their appropriate contexts
Explain how pricing objectives influence pricing decisions
Analyse pricing decisions for a Nigerian product
content: Product: anything offered to the market that might satisfy a want or need; tangible goods, services, ideas, experiences, persons, places
Product levels: core (fundamental benefit), actual/tangible (physical features, brand, packaging), augmented (after-sales service, warranty, delivery)

Product life cycle (PLC): Introduction (low sales, high cost, no profit), Growth (rapid sales increase, profits emerge), Maturity (sales peak, competitive pricing), Decline (falling sales, reduce costs or withdraw)
New product development stages: idea generation, idea screening, concept testing, business analysis, product development, test marketing, commercialisation
Brand: name, symbol, design identifying a seller's product; brand equity — value of brand recognition
Branding decisions: individual brand (each product has own name), family brand (all products under one name), co-branding
Packaging: contains, protects, promotes and provides information; secondary packaging for display
Labelling: brand name, ingredients, weight, instructions, expiry date, manufacturer's details
Pricing objectives: profit maximisation, market share growth, survival (in crisis), quality leadership
Cost-based pricing: cost-plus (add markup to total cost); break-even pricing
Demand-based pricing: high demand → higher price; psychological pricing (₦999 instead of ₦1,000)
Competition-based pricing: match, undercut or price above competitors
Penetration pricing: very low price to gain market share quickly; used for new products in competitive markets
Price skimming: high initial price, gradually reduced; used for innovative products with few competitors
activities: Plot the product life cycle of Nokia mobile phones from 1995 to 2020, identifying which stage applies in 2000, 2007, 2012, and 2020
Compare the branding strategy of Dangote Group (family brand) with Procter & Gamble Nigeria (individual brands for Ariel, Pampers, etc.)
Calculate the break-even price for a student selling zobo drinks: ₦5,000 fixed cost, ₦200 per bottle variable cost, aiming to sell 100 bottles
exam_focus: WAEC tests PLC stages with characteristics, pricing strategy identification in scenarios, and branding types
Know: penetration pricing = low initial price (to grow market share); price skimming = high initial price (for innovation)
Trap: students confuse stages of PLC — in the DECLINE stage, profits fall and companies must decide to reinvest, reformulate or withdraw

topics.topic: Fundamental Economic Concepts and Economic Systems
learning_objectives: Define economics and explain the basic economic problem of scarcity and choice
Distinguish between microeconomics and macroeconomics
Explain opportunity cost and the production possibility curve
Compare the three main economic systems (free market, planned, mixed)
Apply the concept of scale of preference to decision-making
content: Economics: the study of how individuals and societies allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants
Scarcity: resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise) are limited; wants are unlimited
The three basic economic questions: What to produce? How to produce? For whom to produce?
Scale of preference: ranking of wants in order of priority; basis of rational decision-making
Opportunity cost: the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made; not just money — it is the best alternative given up
Production possibility curve (PPC/PPF): shows maximum combinations of two goods produceable with given resources; points on curve = efficient; inside = inefficient; outside = currently unattainable
Microeconomics: study of individual units — households, firms, markets, prices
Macroeconomics: study of the economy as a whole — GDP, inflation, unemployment, balance of payments
Free market (capitalist) economy: private ownership; price mechanism allocates resources; Adam Smith's 'invisible hand'; pros: efficiency, choice; cons: inequality, market failures
Planned (command/socialist) economy: government owns/controls production; central planning; pros: equality; cons: inefficiency, lack of incentives
Mixed economy: combination of free market and government intervention; Nigeria operates a mixed economy

Factors of production: Land (natural resources, reward = rent), Labour (human effort, reward = wages), Capital (manufactured resources, reward = interest), Enterprise/Entrepreneurship (organising the other three, reward = profit)
activities: Draw a production possibility curve for Nigeria choosing between oil production and food production; identify the opportunity cost of increasing oil production
Class survey: each student lists their scale of preference for spending ₦5,000 pocket money; compare and discuss individual vs. group preferences
Debate: 'A free market economy is better for Nigeria than a mixed economy' — use real examples from Nigerian economic policy
exam_focus: WAEC tests PPC interpretation, opportunity cost definition and calculation, and comparison of economic systems
JAMB tests scale of preference, factor of production classification, and free vs. planned economy characteristics
Trap: opportunity cost is NOT the monetary cost — it is the specific best alternative foregone; always state WHAT was given up, not just 'the cost'

learning_objectives: Define demand and supply and state their laws
Distinguish between change in quantity demanded and change in demand
Identify and explain the factors that shift demand and supply curves
Determine market equilibrium price and quantity graphically and algebraically
Explain and calculate price, income and cross elasticities of demand
content: Demand: quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price in a given time period
Law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls (inverse relationship); ceteris paribus
Demand curve: downward sloping; moves along curve (price change); shifts when other factors change
Determinants of demand (shift factors): income, prices of related goods, tastes, expectations, number of buyers
Normal goods (income up → demand up); inferior goods (income up → demand down); Giffen goods (price up → demand up — very rare)
Supply: quantity producers are willing and able to sell at a given price
Law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises (positive relationship); ceteris paribus
Supply curve: upward sloping; determinants: cost of production, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of sellers, climate (agricultural goods)
Market equilibrium: where demand = supply; price clears the market; excess demand (shortage) pushes price up; excess supply (surplus) pushes price down
Algebraically: set Qd = Qs to find equilibrium P and Q
Price elasticity of demand (PED): % change in Qd / % change in P; elastic (|PED|>1) vs. inelastic (|PED|<1); unit elastic (|PED|=1)
Determinants of PED: substitutes available, necessity vs. luxury, proportion of income, time period
Income elasticity of demand (YED): % ΔQd / % ΔY; positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods
Cross elasticity of demand (XED): % ΔQd of A / % ΔP of B; positive = substitutes; negative = complements
activities: Draw demand and supply curves for tomatoes in Lagos; shift the supply curve leftward (drought); find new equilibrium and explain the price change
Given Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 20 + 3P, find equilibrium price and quantity algebraically, then graph both curves
Calculate PED for a product where price rises from ₦50 to ₦60 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 160 units; interpret the result for a business
exam_focus: WAEC tests demand/supply diagram drawing, shift factor identification, equilibrium calculation, and elasticity classification from PED values
JAMB tests law of demand/supply, determinant identification, and PED/YED/XED sign interpretation
Trap: a 'change in demand' (curve shifts) is different from 'change in quantity demanded' (movement along same curve) — price causes movement; other factors cause shifts

topics.topic: National Income — GDP, GNP and Measurement
learning_objectives: Define national income and related concepts (GDP, GNP, NNP, per capita income)
Describe the three methods of measuring national income
Explain the circular flow of income model
Identify difficulties in measuring national income in Nigeria
Interpret national income data for comparing living standards
content: National income: total monetary value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year
GDP (Gross Domestic Product): value of all final goods/services produced within a country's borders in a year
GNP (Gross National Product): GDP + net factor income from abroad (income of citizens abroad − income of foreigners locally)
NNP (Net National Product): GNP − depreciation (capital consumption allowance)
Per capita income: national income / population; used to compare living standards between countries
Expenditure method: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) [consumption + investment + government spending + net exports]
Income method: sum of all factor incomes (wages + rent + interest + profit)
Output method: sum of value added at each stage of production (to avoid double counting)
Value added: selling price − cost of inputs at each stage
Circular flow of income: households supply factors to firms; firms pay factor income; households spend on goods; injections (I, G, X) and withdrawals (S, T, M)

Limitations of national income measurement in Nigeria: subsistence sector (unrecorded), informal economy, non-monetary transactions, uneven distribution (Gini coefficient), quality of life not captured
GDP per capita vs. HDI (Human Development Index): HDI also considers education and health, not just income
Real vs. nominal GDP: nominal measured at current prices; real adjusted for inflation using GDP deflator
activities: Calculate Nigeria's GDP using expenditure method given: C=₦85tr, I=₦20tr, G=₦18tr, X=₦30tr, M=₦25tr
Compare GDP per capita vs. HDI rankings for 5 countries; explain why a high-GDP country may rank lower on HDI
Identify 5 economic activities in your local market not captured in official Nigerian GDP figures; explain why
exam_focus: WAEC tests GDP/GNP distinction, the expenditure formula C+I+G+(X−M), and limitations of national income measurement in Nigeria
JAMB tests definition matching, GDP calculation from given data, and circular flow diagram interpretation
Trap: GDP vs. GNP — GDP is where production occurs (within borders); GNP is who produces (citizens, wherever they are)

learning_objectives: Define and measure inflation using the Consumer Price Index
Identify types and causes of inflation
Distinguish between types of unemployment and their causes
Describe the characteristics of developing economies like Nigeria
Evaluate government policies to control inflation and unemployment
content: Inflation: general and sustained rise in the price level; reduces purchasing power of money
Consumer Price Index (CPI): measures change in price of a basket of goods; inflation rate = (CPI_current − CPI_base)/CPI_base × 100
Types of inflation: creeping (<3% — mild), walking (3–10%), galloping (10–50%), hyperinflation (>50%)
Demand-pull inflation: too much money chasing too few goods; AD > AS; common when government prints money
Cost-push inflation: supply-side shocks (rising wages, raw material cost, oil prices) push prices up
Stagflation: simultaneous high inflation AND high unemployment (worst scenario for policymakers)
Effects of inflation: erodes savings, helps debtors, hurts fixed income earners, reduces exports competitiveness
Unemployment: economically active people who are willing and able to work but cannot find jobs
Types: frictional (between jobs), structural (mismatch of skills), cyclical (recession), seasonal (agricultural/tourism)
Unemployment in Nigeria: graduate unemployment, rural-urban migration, skill mismatch, oil dependency
Government policies: monetary policy (CBN sets interest rates, money supply), fiscal policy (taxation, government spending), supply-side policies (education, infrastructure investment)
Economic development vs. growth: growth = increase in GDP; development = increase in living standards, education, health and equality
Characteristics of underdevelopment: low per capita income, high population growth, subsistence agriculture, low industrialisation, high dependence on primary commodities
activities: Track the Nigerian inflation rate for the past 6 months using NBS data; plot a graph and identify the trend
Calculate CPI if a basket costing ₦5,000 in base year now costs ₦6,200; calculate the inflation rate
Role-play: the CBN Monetary Policy Committee decides whether to raise or cut interest rates in response to 25% inflation — argue both sides
exam_focus: WAEC tests inflation types, CPI calculation, unemployment types, and government anti-inflation policies
JAMB tests inflation definition, demand-pull vs. cost-push distinction, and unemployment type identification
Trap: inflation rate measures the RATE OF CHANGE of prices, not the absolute price level — prices rising at 10% means inflation is 10%, not that prices rose by ₦10

topics.topic: The State, Sovereignty and Government Systems
learning_objectives: Define the state, government and politics
Explain the elements of the state (population, territory, government, sovereignty)
Distinguish between systems of government (democracy, authoritarianism, military)
Compare federalism, unitary and confederal systems
Explain the functions of government and limits on governmental power
content: State: politically organized community occupying a definite territory with a government and sovereignty
Four elements of the state: population (people), territory (defined area), government (authority to rule), sovereignty (supreme power, internal and external)
Government: institutions and processes through which the state exercises authority
Functions of government: making laws, enforcing laws, adjudicating disputes, maintaining security, providing public goods, managing the economy
Democracy: rule by the people; direct (ancient Athens) and representative/indirect (modern states)
Principles of democracy: majority rule, minority rights, rule of law, separation of powers, free and fair elections, civilian supremacy
Authoritarianism: concentrated power; limited political pluralism; Nigeria's military regimes (Yakubu Gowon, Murtala, Buhari/Idiagbon, Babangida, Abacha)
Federalism: division of powers between central and state governments; written constitution; Nigeria, USA, India are federal
Unitary system: central government supreme; local governments derive powers from centre; France, UK
Confederal system: loose alliance of independent states; central authority very weak; e.g. Confederation of 1781 (USA before Constitution)
Separation of powers: executive, legislature and judiciary exercise different powers; prevents tyranny (Montesquieu)
Checks and balances: each arm limits the other's power; e.g. legislature approves executive appointments; judiciary can declare legislation unconstitutional
activities: Create a comparison table for federal, unitary and confederal systems on 5 criteria: location of sovereignty, examples, constitutional arrangement, pros, cons
Map all military heads of state in Nigeria from independence to 1999; identify the coup dates and reasons given
Debate: 'Nigerian democracy has failed the ordinary citizen since 1999' — argue pro and con using evidence
exam_focus: WAEC tests elements of the state, differences between federalism and unitary systems, functions of government, and separation of powers
JAMB tests definitions, federalism characteristics, and principles of democracy — memorise the four elements of the state
Trap: sovereignty is the MOST important element of the state — without sovereignty, the state cannot exist (unlike population alone, which could just be a group of people)

topics.topic: Nigerian Constitution and the Three Tiers of Government
learning_objectives: Describe the features and significance of the Nigerian Constitution
Identify and explain the three tiers and three arms of government in Nigeria
Analyse the distribution of powers under the 1999 Constitution
Explain the roles of INEC, judiciary and civil service in Nigerian governance
Evaluate the practice of federalism in Nigeria
content: Constitution: fundamental law of the land; supreme over all other laws in Nigeria; 1999 Constitution (as amended)
Features of Nigerian constitution: written (codified), rigid (requires special procedure to amend), supreme (other laws are void if inconsistent), federal
Constitutional supremacy: Section 1 of 1999 Constitution declares it supreme
Three tiers: Federal (Abuja), State (36 states + FCT), Local Government (774 LGAs)

Three arms of government: Executive (President/Governor/Chairman — implements laws), Legislature (National Assembly/State House of Assembly/Legislative Council — makes laws), Judiciary (Federal Supreme Court/State High Court — interprets laws)
Exclusive legislative list: only Federal Government can legislate (defence, immigration, customs, currency, aviation)
Concurrent list: both Federal and State can legislate; federal law prevails in conflict (education, health, agriculture)
Residual powers: what is not listed goes to states
INEC (Independent National Electoral Commission): conducts federal and state elections; registers voters and parties; established by Section 153 of 1999 Constitution
Revenue allocation: FAAC (Federal Account Allocation Committee); sharing formula: Federal (52.68%), States (26.72%), LGA (20.60%) as of recent revisions
Challenges of Nigerian federalism: fiscal federalism imbalance, derivation principle debates, state creation, rotational presidency
activities: Map the exclusive, concurrent and residual legislative lists from the 1999 Constitution; classify 20 functions into the correct list
Trace how a bill becomes law in Nigeria: from introduction in the House of Representatives through Senate, President assent, to gazette
Case study: evaluate how INEC managed the 2023 General Elections — what worked, what failed, and what reforms are needed
exam_focus: WAEC tests exclusive vs. concurrent legislative lists with examples, features of Nigerian constitution, and INEC's roles
JAMB tests powers of each tier of government, constitutional supremacy, and arm of government functions
Trap: only FEDERAL government can legislate on the EXCLUSIVE list; both can legislate on the CONCURRENT list — states cannot touch exclusive matters

topics.topic: Political Parties and Electoral Process in Nigeria
learning_objectives: Define a political party and explain its functions
Trace the history of political parties in Nigeria from 1923 to present
Explain the Nigerian electoral process from registration to declaration of results
Evaluate the challenges of elections in Nigeria
Explain the role of pressure groups and civil society
content: Political party: organized group of people with similar political views seeking to win power through elections
Functions of political parties: political education, recruitment of political leaders, forming government, aggregating interests, political socialization

History of Nigerian political parties: NNDP (1923 — Macaulay), NYM (1934), NCNC (1944 — Azikiwe), AG (1950 — Awolowo), NPC (1949 — Bello); 2nd Republic: NPN, UPN, NPP, GNPP, PRP; 3rd Republic: NRC, SDP; 4th Republic: PDP (dominant 1999–2015), APC (formed 2013, won 2015), others (LP, NNPP)
Party system types: one-party (authoritarian), two-party (USA, UK), multi-party (Nigeria, Germany)
Electoral process: voter registration → party primaries → campaign → polling day → collation → declaration → petition (if any)
Types of electoral systems: first-past-the-post (FPTP — Nigeria), proportional representation, alternative vote
Electoral malpractice: ballot stuffing, voter intimidation, underage voting, result manipulation
Electoral reforms: Uwais Commission (2008), Independent Candidacy, BVAS (Bimodal Voter Accreditation System) introduced 2023
Pressure groups: organisations that influence government policy without seeking power; NLC, NBA, NMA, NANS
Civil society: non-governmental organisations (NGOs), media, religious bodies; watchdogs of democracy
activities: Create a timeline of Nigerian political parties from 1922 to 2023, identifying founding date, leader, region of support and key elections contested
Mock election: class forms two parties, campaigns, votes, and conducts a mini-election using INEC procedures; identify lessons learned
Analyse: how did the introduction of BVAS technology in 2023 change the Nigerian electoral experience? Were results more credible?
exam_focus: WAEC tests party history (founders, years, regions), functions of political parties, and the electoral process step by step
JAMB tests party founders, definitions, pressure group vs. political party distinction
Key names to memorise: Macaulay (NNDP), Azikiwe (NCNC), Awolowo (AG/UPN), Ahmadu Bello (NPC), Balewa (PM 1960)

topics.topic: Nigeria's Foreign Policy and International Organizations
learning_objectives: Define foreign policy and explain Nigeria's foreign policy objectives
Describe Nigeria's role in African and world affairs
Explain the structure and functions of the United Nations
Describe the African Union and ECOWAS and their roles
Evaluate Nigeria's contributions to peacekeeping and international development
content: Foreign policy: a country's strategy and actions toward other nations; guides diplomatic, economic and military relations

Nigeria's foreign policy principles: African-centred policy (Africa as centrepiece), non-alignment (colonial era), non-interference in internal affairs of states, promotion of democracy and human rights, support for UN/AU/ECOWAS
Nigeria's foreign policy history: Black Africa centrepiece (Balewa, Gowon era), Southward Look (supporting anti-apartheid), Northward Look, Citizen-centred diplomacy (4th Republic)
United Nations (UN): established 1945 after WWII; 193 member states; headquarters New York; principal organs: General Assembly, Security Council, Secretariat, ICJ, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council
UN Security Council: 5 permanent members (USA, UK, France, Russia, China — P5 with veto power) + 10 rotating members; primary responsibility for international peace
UN Specialized Agencies: UNESCO, WHO, ILO, UNICEF, FAO, UNHCR, World Bank, IMF
African Union (AU): successor to OAU; established 2002; headquarters Addis Ababa; 55 members; promotes African unity, peace and development; AU Commission, African Court of Human Rights, NEPAD
ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States): established 1975, Lagos; 16 West African nations; promotes economic integration, ECOWAS Passport, ECOMOG peacekeeping
Nigeria's peacekeeping: ECOMOG in Liberia (1990) and Sierra Leone; UN missions worldwide; largest contributor to African Union peacekeeping
Commonwealth of Nations: 56 countries; former British empire; promotes democracy, development, rule of law
activities: Map Nigeria's peacekeeping contributions from 1960 to present: list the countries, years and outcomes of each ECOMOG/UN mission
Evaluate Nigeria's 'Africa as centrepiece' foreign policy: three successes (e.g. anti-apartheid support, ECOWAS leadership) and three failures (Bakassi Peninsula cession, brain drain)
Role-play a UN Security Council debate on a current African conflict; assign P5 roles and veto power to understand UN decision-making
exam_focus: WAEC tests Nigeria's foreign policy principles, UN organs and their functions, ECOWAS objectives, and Nigeria's peacekeeping role
JAMB tests founding of UN/AU/ECOWAS, Security Council membership (P5), and Nigeria's international role
Trap: OAU (founded 1963) became the AU (2002) — they are not the same organisation; ECOWAS was founded in 1975, NOT 1963

learning_objectives: Define poetry and distinguish it from prose
Identify and explain major forms of poetry (lyric, narrative, dramatic, epic, dramatic monologue)
Analyse poetic devices in unseen and prescribed poems
Write a critical appreciation of a given poem using a structured framework
Compare two or more poems on the basis of theme, style and language
content: Poetry: literary art form using compressed, rhythmic language to convey emotion, ideas and images; exploits sound and meaning simultaneously
Lyric poetry: expresses personal emotion (ode, elegy, sonnet); first-person; subjective
Narrative poetry: tells a story (ballad, epic); has plot, characters, setting
Dramatic poetry: spoken by a character/persona in a specific situation; dramatic monologue
Sonnet: 14-line poem; Shakespearean (3 quatrains + couplet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG) vs. Petrarchan (octave + sestet, ABBAABBA CDECDE)
Ballad: narrative folk poem; simple stanzas, refrain, oral tradition origins
Ode: formal poem addressed to a subject; elevated language; Pindaric, Horatian, Irregular
Free verse: no regular rhyme or metre; modern poetry; relies on imagery and line breaks
Poetic devices: alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole, oxymoron, paradox, irony, symbolism, imagery, refrain, enjambment, caesura
Prosody: metre (iambic pentameter most common in English — 5 iambic feet per line), rhyme scheme (ABAB, AABB, etc.), rhythm
Tone: poet's attitude (e.g. melancholic, celebratory, satirical, nostalgic)
Critical appreciation framework: Speaker/persona, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject/Theme, Tone/Mood, Language/Style, Form/Structure, Overall Effect
activities: Read J.P. Clark's 'Abiku' and Wole Soyinka's 'Abiku' — compare how each poet treats the same Nigerian concept using different forms and devices
Write a 400-word critical appreciation of an unseen poem, applying the SOAPS framework with textual evidence
Write an original 14-line sonnet on a topic of your choice; include at least 3 named poetic devices
exam_focus: WAEC (Essay 1 and 2) and JAMB test: close reading of prescribed texts, identification of devices WITH explanation of their effect, theme analysis
Always QUOTE from the poem when identifying a device — an identified device without quotation scores no marks in WAEC
Trap: confusing simile (uses 'like' or 'as') with metaphor (direct comparison without 'like' or 'as') — be precise in labelling

learning_objectives: Define drama and distinguish between dramatic text and performance
Identify and explain the elements of drama
Analyse characterisation, conflict and theme in prescribed plays
Distinguish between tragedy, comedy and tragicomedy
Write a critical essay on a prescribed dramatic text
content: Drama: literary form meant to be performed on stage; combines dialogue, action and spectacle
Elements of drama: plot, character, theme, dialogue, stagecraft (setting, lighting, costume, sound), conflict
Plot structure: exposition, rising action, climax (turning point), falling action, denouement
Types of conflict: protagonist vs. antagonist; person vs. self (internal); person vs. society; person vs. fate
Characterisation: protagonist (hero/main character), antagonist (villain/opposition), foil (contrast to protagonist); flat vs. round characters; static vs. dynamic
Tragedy: ends in the protagonist's downfall/death; hamartia (tragic flaw); catharsis (emotional release); Shakespearean vs. Greek tragedy
Comedy: ends happily; satirical (lampoons society), romantic (love complications), farce (exaggerated humour)
Tragicomedy: blends elements of both; common in modern African drama
Dramatic irony: audience knows something characters do not; creates tension
Soliloquy: character speaking thoughts aloud alone on stage
Aside: character speaks to audience without other characters hearing
Stage directions: instructions about setting, movement, delivery — usually in brackets/italics in text
African drama: Wole Soyinka, J.P. Clark, Ola Rotimi — blend Yoruba, Ijaw traditions with Western form; oral tradition, ritual, ancestor spirits
activities: Stage a 10-minute excerpt from a prescribed play; class critiques performance on characterisation, conflict, and theme
Write a character analysis essay of one major and one minor character in a prescribed play: background, motivation, development, significance
Compare how 'Death and the King's Horseman' (Soyinka) and a Western tragedy handle the concept of fatalism/duty
exam_focus: WAEC Drama questions test: plot summary accuracy, character analysis with evidence, theme identification and exploration, and dramatic devices
JAMB tests terminology (soliloquy, aside, dramatic irony), character roles, and conflict types
Trap: confusing a PLAY'S THEME (central message) with its SUBJECT (topic) — theme is the MEANING or lesson; subject is what it is about

topics.topic: Prose Fiction — Novel and Short Story
learning_objectives: Define prose fiction and distinguish between the novel and short story
Analyse the narrative elements of prescribed prose texts
Evaluate the theme, style and significance of prescribed novels
Write an essay discussing aspects of a prescribed prose text with evidence
Compare African and non-African prose on themes of colonialism, identity and development
content: Prose fiction: narrative accounts of imaginary events told in free-flowing prose; genre of literature
Novel: long prose narrative with developed plot, characters and setting; major world form from 18th century
Short story: brief prose narrative; usually one main conflict, limited characters, single effect

Narrative point of view: first-person narrator (uses 'I'; subjective), third-person omniscient (knows all characters' thoughts), third-person limited (knows one character), second-person (uses 'you' — rare)
Narrative techniques: flashback, foreshadowing, stream of consciousness, unreliable narrator, epistolary (told through letters)
Setting: time (historical period, season, time of day) and place; creates atmosphere; symbolic settings
Theme: central message; may be about love, conflict, identity, colonialism, corruption, family, social justice
Style: author's distinctive use of language, syntax, tone, imagery, rhythm; African writers often blend oral tradition
African novel tradition: Chinua Achebe (Things Fall Apart — colonialism, Igbo culture), Chimamanda Adichie (Purple Hibiscus, Half of a Yellow Sun), Wole Soyinka, Ngugi wa Thiong'o
Motif: recurring image, symbol or idea that reinforces theme
Symbolism: objects, characters or events representing abstract ideas (e.g. the yam in TFA = Igbo manhood)
Critical essay structure: introduction (text, author, central argument), body paragraphs (point + evidence + analysis), conclusion (significance)
activities: Write a 600-word essay on ONE theme in a prescribed novel, supporting each point with at least two specific textual references
Create a character relationship map for a prescribed novel: show how characters are connected and how those relationships develop
Compare the treatment of 'cultural conflict' in Achebe's Things Fall Apart and any other prescribed African text
exam_focus: WAEC Prose essay tests: direct knowledge of prescribed texts, analytical writing with embedded quotations, and structured argument
JAMB tests factual knowledge of characters, events and author details from prescribed texts
Critical rule: never retell the story — ANALYSE it; the examiner has read the book; your job is to evaluate, not summarise

topics.topic: Exercise Physiology — Cardiovascular and Respiratory Responses
learning_objectives: Describe the structure and function of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems
Explain the body's acute and chronic responses to exercise
Measure and interpret resting and exercise heart rate, blood pressure and breathing rate
Explain the concepts of aerobic and anaerobic exercise and their energy systems
Relate regular exercise to cardiovascular health
content: Cardiovascular system: heart (4 chambers — RA, RV, LA, LV), blood vessels (arteries carry blood away from heart; veins carry back; capillaries exchange gases/nutrients), blood (plasma, erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets)
Cardiac output: Q = heart rate × stroke volume; average resting: ~5 L/min; during intense exercise: up to 25 L/min
Heart rate: normal resting 60–100 bpm; trained athletes may have resting HR of 40–50 bpm (bradycardia — adaptation)
Blood pressure: systolic (contraction)/diastolic (relaxation); normal ≈120/80 mmHg
Respiratory system: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli; alveoli = site of gas exchange (O₂ in, CO₂ out)
Tidal volume: air breathed in one breath (~500 mL at rest); increases during exercise
Minute ventilation: tidal volume × breathing rate; increases dramatically during exercise

Acute responses to exercise: increased HR, increased stroke volume, increased cardiac output, increased breathing rate, increased tidal volume, vasodilation of muscles, vasoconstriction of non-working organs
Chronic adaptations to training: lower resting HR, larger stroke volume, stronger heart muscle (cardiac hypertrophy), increased lung capacity, increased blood volume, more efficient O₂ use
Energy systems: ATP-PC system (0–10 seconds, explosive activities), glycolytic/lactic acid system (10 seconds–2 minutes, anaerobic), aerobic oxidative system (>2 minutes, endurance)
VO₂ max: maximum rate of oxygen consumption; gold standard of cardiovascular fitness
Lifestyle diseases prevented by exercise: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obesity, coronary heart disease, some cancers
activities: Measure resting HR and BP for 5 classmates; have them jog for 5 minutes; re-measure immediately after and 5 minutes after; graph recovery
Design a 12-week aerobic training programme for a hypertensive adult, specifying mode, intensity (THR zone), duration and frequency per week
Calculate target heart rate (THR) zone using Karvonen formula: THR = (HRmax − HRrest) × intensity% + HRrest
exam_focus: WAEC tests cardiovascular anatomy, acute vs. chronic training adaptations, energy system identification from activity type
Know: aerobic exercise uses oxygen (long duration, moderate intensity); anaerobic does not (short duration, high intensity)
Trap: 'resting heart rate decreasing with training' is a CHRONIC adaptation (long-term change), not an acute response to a single exercise bout

learning_objectives: Define health and explain the WHO definition of health
Identify major lifestyle diseases prevalent in Nigeria and their risk factors
Design and promote health behaviour change programmes
Explain the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion
Evaluate nutrition's role in health and athletic performance
content: WHO definition of health (1948): 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'
Health dimensions: physical, mental/psychological, social, emotional, spiritual, environmental

Health promotion: enabling people to increase control over their health; Ottawa Charter (1986) strategies: building healthy public policy, creating supportive environments, strengthening community action, developing personal skills, reorienting health services
Lifestyle diseases (non-communicable diseases — NCDs): caused by behaviours; not infectious; major cause of death in Nigeria increasingly
Hypertension: persistent BP >140/90 mmHg; risk factors: obesity, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, high sodium diet, stress; prevention: exercise, low-salt diet, reduce alcohol
Type 2 diabetes: insufficient insulin response; risk factors: obesity, physical inactivity, poor diet; prevention: weight control, exercise, healthy diet
Obesity: BMI ≥30; associated with hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, joint problems; causes: excessive caloric intake + insufficient physical activity
Coronary Heart Disease (CHD): atherosclerosis (plaque in coronary arteries); risk factors: smoking, high LDL cholesterol, hypertension, obesity
Cancer: uncontrolled cell growth; lifestyle-related: lung cancer (smoking), colorectal cancer (low fibre diet), skin cancer (UV exposure)
Nutrition for athletes: macronutrients (CHO for energy — 60% of diet; protein for muscle repair — 1.2–2.0 g/kg; fat for energy and hormones), micronutrients, hydration (water loss through sweat)
Carbohydrate loading: strategy to maximize glycogen stores before endurance events
Eating disorders: anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa — serious mental health conditions with physical consequences
activities: Conduct a health risk factor survey in the school: measure BMI for 20 students; identify the percentage that fall in healthy, overweight and obese categories
Design a community health promotion campaign for Diabetes Day (November 14) targeting a Lagos secondary school population
Analyse a Nigerian athlete's training diet; identify nutritional deficiencies and recommend improvements using Nigeria's food composition table
exam_focus: WAEC tests WHO definition, lifestyle disease risk factors and prevention, and Ottawa Charter health promotion strategies
Know BMI classification: Underweight <18.5, Normal 18.5–24.9, Overweight 25–29.9, Obese ≥30
Trap: lifestyle diseases are NOT infectious and cannot be spread from person to person — they are caused by individual behaviour and genetics

learning_objectives: Describe the structure of sports administration at local, national and international levels
Explain the roles of major Nigerian and international sports organisations
Identify the principles of effective sports administration
Plan and organise a school sports competition
Evaluate the roles of government in sports development
content: Sports administration: management of sports organisations, facilities, programmes and personnel for optimal performance and development
Levels of sports administration: grassroots/school level, state, national (NSF — National Sports Federation), international (IFs — International Federations)

Nigerian sports organisations: NSC (National Sports Commission), NFF (Nigeria Football Federation), NBBF (Nigeria Basketball Federation), Athletics Federation of Nigeria (AFN), NOC (National Olympic Committee of Nigeria)

International organisations: IOC (International Olympic Committee — Paris; governs Olympic Games; founded 1894); FIFA (football — Zurich; founded 1904); IAAF/World Athletics (athletics); FIBA (basketball); CAF (Confederation of African Football)
African sports organisations: CAF (African football), ANOCA (African National Olympic Committees), CANA (African aquatics)
Principles of sports administration: planning, organising, directing, controlling, staffing (PODCS)
Types of tournaments: round robin (league system — everyone plays everyone), knock-out/elimination, combination, double elimination
Planning a sports competition: objectives, schedule, budget, venues, officials, rules, prizes, transport, safety
NSSF (National School Sports Federation) — organises inter-school sports in Nigeria
Government's role in sports: funding, policy, facilities, talent identification, international representation, anti-doping
Sports funding in Nigeria: government allocation, sponsorship, sports lottery, FIFA/IOC grants
Volunteerism and sports: role of volunteers in grassroots development
activities: Organise a class mini-tournament in any sport using a round-robin format: draw up fixtures, record results, calculate points and rank teams
Create an organisational chart of Nigerian football administration from FIFA → CAF → NFF → State FAs → Clubs
Write a proposal for a sports festival at your school: include objectives, programme, budget, officials needed, and safety plan
exam_focus: WAEC tests functions of sports organisations (NOC, NSF, NFF), tournament types, and principles of sports administration
Know: IOC (Olympic Games), FIFA (football), IAAF (athletics), FIBA (basketball), ITF (tennis)
Trap: NSC (National Sports Commission) is a government agency; NOC (National Olympic Committee) is a non-governmental body representing Nigeria at the Olympics — different entities

topics.topic: Sports Medicine — Injuries, First Aid and Prevention
learning_objectives: Classify sports injuries and explain their causes
Apply basic first aid procedures for common sports injuries
Explain the RICE/PRICE principle for soft tissue injury management
Describe warm-up and cool-down as injury prevention strategies
Identify banned substances and explain anti-doping policies
content: Sports injuries classification: acute (sudden onset — fracture, strain, sprain, contusion, laceration) vs. chronic/overuse (gradual onset — shin splints, stress fracture, tendinitis, bursitis)
Sprain: ligament injury (connects bone to bone); graded I (mild), II (partial tear), III (complete tear)
Strain: muscle or tendon injury; most common: hamstring strain, calf strain
Fracture types: closed (skin intact), open/compound (bone penetrates skin), stress (hairline crack from repeated loading)
Dislocation: bones of a joint forced out of alignment; common: shoulder, fingers
PRICE principle: Protect, Rest, Ice (20 min on/off), Compression, Elevation — for acute soft tissue injuries
DR ABC in emergency: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation — emergency assessment order
CPR: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation; 30 compressions (5–6 cm depth, 100–120/min) : 2 breaths ratio
Heat-related illness: heat cramps (muscle cramps due to dehydration), heat exhaustion (weakness, dizziness), heat stroke (medical emergency — confusion, collapse, high core temp)
Warm-up: 10–15 minutes; gradually increases body temperature and heart rate; reduces injury risk; includes general (aerobic) and specific (sport-related) components
Cool-down: returns body to resting state; prevents blood pooling; static stretching for flexibility
Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs): anabolic steroids, EPO (blood doping), stimulants, diuretics, HGH
WADA (World Anti-Doping Agency): sets prohibited list; in-competition and out-of-competition testing; Nigeria Anti-Doping Agency (NADA)
activities: Simulate a sports first aid scenario: one student 'sprains their ankle' during a football game; class applies PRICE treatment step by step
Demonstrate and practise CPR on a mannequin or cushion: compression depth, rate and rescue breath technique
Create a poster for the school changing room: 'Top 5 ways to prevent sports injuries' — include warm-up, equipment, hydration, technique and rest
exam_focus: WAEC tests injury classification, RICE/PRICE procedure, DR ABC order, and warm-up/cool-down purposes
Know: sprain = ligament; strain = muscle/tendon — a common exam distinction
Trap: ICE is for ACUTE injuries (within 48 hours); HEAT is for CHRONIC injuries (after 48 hours) — applying heat to a fresh sprain makes it worse

learning_objectives: Read, write and compare whole numbers up to one billion
Perform the four operations on whole numbers, fractions and decimals
Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages
Apply BODMAS/PEMDAS rule to simplify expressions
Solve word problems involving numbers in everyday contexts
content: Place value: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, millions, billions
Roman numerals: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000
Types of fractions: proper (n<d), improper (n≥d), mixed numbers
Operations on fractions: addition/subtraction (common denominator), multiplication (straight across), division (multiply by reciprocal)
Decimals: place value system extended; adding zeros for alignment
Converting fractions to decimals: divide numerator by denominator
Converting decimals to fractions: place value denominator, simplify
Percentages: means 'out of 100'; x% = x/100
Percentage of a quantity: % × amount; percentage increase/decrease
BODMAS: Brackets, Order (powers), Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction
LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) and HCF (Highest Common Factor): prime factorisation method
Word problems: key words (total, difference, product, quotient, per, of)
activities: Use fraction strips to visually add 1/3 + 1/4; verify algebraically
Convert the class's test scores to percentages, fractions and decimals; rank in order
Apply BODMAS to 5 multi-operation expressions and compare answers with classmates
exam_focus: BECE tests all four operations with fractions and decimals, percentage calculations, and BODMAS — show all working
Know the key percentage relationships: 25% = 1/4, 50% = 1/2, 75% = 3/4, 10% = 1/10, 20% = 1/5
Trap: in BODMAS, Division and Multiplication have equal priority (left to right); same for Addition and Subtraction — do NOT always divide before multiplying

topics.topic: Integers, Directed Numbers and Number Lines
learning_objectives: Define integers and distinguish positive, negative and zero
Perform operations on directed (positive and negative) numbers
Use a number line to represent and compare integers
Apply directed numbers to real-life situations (temperature, profit/loss, sea level)
content: Integers: whole numbers; positive (1, 2, 3...), zero (0), negative (...−3, −2, −1)
Number line: negative numbers to the left of zero; positive to the right
Comparing integers: further left = smaller; −7 < −2
Adding integers: same sign → add, keep sign; different signs → subtract smaller from larger, keep sign of larger
Subtracting integers: change sign of subtracted number and add; e.g. 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8
Multiplying/dividing integers: same signs → positive product; different signs → negative product
Real-life applications: temperature (above/below zero °C), altitude (above/below sea level), profit/loss, deposits/withdrawals
Absolute value: |n| = distance from zero; always non-negative; |−5| = 5
Order of operations still applies with negative numbers
activities: Use a vertical number line to model changes in temperature: starts at 5°C, drops 8°C overnight, rises 3°C by noon — what is the final temperature?
Simulate a bank account: ₦500 balance, deposit ₦300, withdraw ₦700, deposit ₦200 — track the balance using directed numbers
Play directed number bingo: teacher calls operations, students compute and mark their boards
exam_focus: BECE tests operations with negative numbers and real-life applications — draw a number line if it helps
Remember: negative × negative = positive; negative × positive = negative
Trap: −2² = −4 (only the 2 is squared, not the negative sign), but (−2)² = +4 (the negative IS squared)

learning_objectives: Write and simplify algebraic expressions
Expand and factorise simple algebraic expressions
Solve simple linear equations in one variable
Set up and solve equations from word problems
Evaluate algebraic expressions by substitution
content: Algebraic expression: combination of variables, coefficients and constants; e.g. 3x + 2y − 5
Term, coefficient, variable, constant: in 5x², '5' is coefficient, 'x' is variable, '²' is power
Like terms: same variable(s) with same power; can be combined; 3x + 5x = 8x
Expanding brackets: multiply each term inside by the factor outside; 3(2x + 4) = 6x + 12
Factorisation: reverse of expansion; find common factor; 6x + 12 = 6(x + 2)
Substitution: replace variable with given number; if a = 3, b = 2: find 2a + b = 2(3) + 2 = 8
Linear equation: highest power of variable is 1; one solution
Solving linear equations: balance principle — whatever you do to one side, do to the other
Steps: expand brackets → collect like terms → isolate variable → divide by coefficient
Word problems: 'a number added to 5 equals 13' → n + 5 = 13; solve for n
Inequalities: < less than, > greater than, ≤ less than or equal, ≥ greater than or equal
Representing inequalities on a number line
activities: Simplify: 3x + 2y − x + 4y − 2; then substitute x = 2, y = 1 to verify
Solve: 2(x + 3) = 14 showing each step; check by substituting back
Write and solve: 'Amaka is 3 years older than Chidi. The sum of their ages is 29. Find each person's age'
exam_focus: BECE tests simplification, expansion, factorisation and solving equations from word problems
Always CHECK your answer by substituting back into the original equation
Trap: when solving 3x = 12, divide BOTH sides by 3 (not subtract) — inverse operation of multiplication is division

topics.topic: Shapes, Angles and Properties of 2D Figures
learning_objectives: Identify and classify angles (acute, right, obtuse, reflex, straight)
Apply angle properties (angles on a line, at a point, in a triangle, in a polygon)
Identify and state properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
Calculate the interior and exterior angle sum of any polygon
Solve geometrical problems involving parallel lines and transversals
content: Types of angles: acute (0°–90°), right (90°), obtuse (90°–180°), straight (180°), reflex (180°–360°), revolution (360°)
Angle relationships: angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles at a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal
Types of triangles: by sides — equilateral (3 equal), isosceles (2 equal), scalene (none equal); by angles — acute, right, obtuse
Triangle angle sum: always 180°

Properties of quadrilaterals: square (4 equal sides, 4 right angles), rectangle (opposite sides equal, 4 right angles), parallelogram (opposite sides parallel and equal), rhombus (4 equal sides), trapezium (1 pair parallel sides), kite (2 pairs adjacent equal sides)
Polygon angle sums: interior angle sum = (n−2) × 180°; exterior angle sum always = 360°
Regular polygon: each interior angle = (n−2) × 180° / n
Parallel lines and transversals: corresponding angles equal (F-shape), alternate angles equal (Z-shape), co-interior (same-side interior) angles supplementary (C-shape)
Construction tools: ruler, compass, protractor; constructing 60°, 90°, bisecting angles and lines
activities: Measure all interior angles of 5 different triangles cut from paper; verify they each sum to 180°
Construct an equilateral triangle using ruler and compass (60° method); then bisect one angle to create 30°
Find all unknown angles in a diagram with two parallel lines cut by a transversal, justifying each step with the correct property name
exam_focus: BECE tests angle calculations, quadrilateral properties, parallel line angle relationships, and polygon interior angle sums
Always state the reason for each angle found: 'alternate angles are equal' not just writing the number
Trap: co-interior angles are SUPPLEMENTARY (sum to 180°), not equal — unlike alternate and corresponding angles which ARE equal

learning_objectives: Calculate perimeter and area of rectangles, triangles, circles and compound shapes
Calculate surface area and volume of cuboids, cylinders and triangular prisms
Solve problems involving area and volume in everyday contexts
Convert between units of length, area and volume
content: Perimeter: total distance around a shape; add all sides
Area of rectangle: l × b; square: l²
Area of triangle: ½ × base × height
Area of parallelogram: base × perpendicular height
Area of trapezium: ½(a + b) × h
Circumference of circle: 2πr or πd; π ≈ 22/7 or 3.142
Area of circle: πr²
Area of sector: (θ/360) × πr²
Arc length: (θ/360) × 2πr
Volume of cuboid: l × b × h
Volume of cylinder: πr²h
Volume of triangular prism: ½ × base × height × length
Surface area: total area of all faces; for cuboid = 2(lb + lh + bh)
Unit conversion: 1 m = 100 cm; 1 km = 1000 m; 1 m² = 10,000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³
activities: Measure the classroom floor; calculate its area and perimeter; estimate how many tiles (30cm × 30cm) are needed
Find the volume of a cylindrical well of radius 0.5 m and depth 10 m; calculate how many litres of water it holds (1 m³ = 1,000 L)
Calculate the area of a compound shape: a rectangle with a semicircle on one end
exam_focus: BECE tests area, perimeter, and volume using standard formulas — always write down the formula before substituting
Use π = 22/7 when radius is a multiple of 7; use π = 3.14 or 3.142 otherwise — check what the question specifies
Trap: area is in square units (cm², m²) and volume in cubic units (cm³, m³) — losing units loses marks

topics.topic: Speech Sounds, Word Stress and Conversational English
learning_objectives: Identify vowel and consonant sounds in English
Apply correct stress in two- and three-syllable words
Distinguish minimal pairs to demonstrate phonemic awareness
Use appropriate conversational register in school and social contexts
Apply turn-taking and listening skills in discussions
content: Vowel sounds: short and long vowels; e.g. /ɪ/ (sit) vs. /iː/ (seat), /æ/ (cat) vs. /ɑː/ (cart)
Consonant sounds: initial, medial and final positions; voiced vs. voiceless pairs (/b/ vs. /p/, /d/ vs. /t/, /g/ vs. /k/)
Minimal pairs: two words differing in only one sound; e.g. bat/bad, fan/van, ship/chip
Word stress in two-syllable words: most nouns stressed on 1st syllable (TABLE, MUsic), most verbs on 2nd (reLAX, obEY)
Sentence stress: content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) stressed; function words (articles, prepositions) unstressed
Intonation: falling (statements, commands), rising (yes/no questions), fall-rise (doubt, encouragement)
Silent letters: kneel (k silent), write (w silent), know (k silent), hour (h silent), lamb (b silent)
Formal greetings: 'Good morning, sir/ma', 'How are you?', 'May I come in?'
Informal greetings and responses: age-appropriate casual language
Taking turns in conversation: listening signals, interrupting politely ('Excuse me, may I add...'), summarising what was said
Role play and conversation practice: at the market, at school, giving directions
activities: Practise minimal pairs in pairs: one student says 'ship' or 'sheep', the other points to the correct picture
Record and play back a reading; identify words with incorrect stress and practise the correct pattern
Role-play a conversation at a bus stop asking for directions to a hospital — practise formal politeness
exam_focus: BECE tests sound identification, stress patterns, and appropriate conversational responses
Know common silent letter words: kneel, write, know, knock, lamb, thumb, hour, honest
Trap: word stress changes meaning — REcord (noun) vs. reCORD (verb); this is tested in BECE

learning_objectives: Apply skimming and scanning in comprehension tasks
Determine word meanings from context
Identify the main idea and supporting details of a passage
Summarise a passage in own words
Infer meaning from figurative language
content: Skimming: reading for general idea; eyes move quickly; note headings, topic sentences, first and last paragraphs
Scanning: searching for specific information; keywords, dates, names; used in research
Topic sentence: sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph; usually first sentence
Main idea: what the whole passage is about; vs. supporting details which give evidence/examples
Context clues: use surrounding words to understand unfamiliar vocabulary
Figurative language: simile (like/as), metaphor (direct comparison), personification (giving human traits to non-human things)
Vocabulary in context: multiple-choice vocabulary tests use the word in a sentence to guide meaning selection
Summary writing: identify 3–5 key points; write in own words; no opinions; one-third of original length
Inference: reading between the lines; use text clues + general knowledge
Text types in comprehension: narrative (story), expository (information), descriptive (describes a scene or person)
activities: Time-limited skim of a 400-word passage (2 minutes); answer 3 main-idea questions without re-reading
Identify the topic sentence and 3 supporting details in each paragraph of a given text
Write a 100-word summary of a 300-word passage; compare with a classmate's version
exam_focus: BECE comprehension tests: ability to find answers in the text (literal), infer meaning (inferential), and understand vocabulary in context
Answer comprehension questions in complete sentences; begin with the key word from the question
Trap: do not copy long chunks from the passage — paraphrase in your own words for full credit

topics.topic: Paragraphing, Letter Writing and Narrative Essays
learning_objectives: Write structured paragraphs with a clear topic sentence
Write a narrative essay with introduction, body and conclusion
Write formal and informal letters with correct layout
Apply correct punctuation and spelling in writing
Identify and correct common errors in written English
