content: Paragraph: unified block of writing on one idea; topic sentence + supporting sentences + concluding/linking sentence
Narrative essay: tells a story; first or third person; chronological order; vivid details; dialogue; climax
Descriptive essay: describes a person, place or event; sensory language; spatial organisation
Informal letter: to a friend or family member; sender's address, date, salutation (Dear Chidi), body, closing (Your friend, ...); chatty, personal tone
Formal letter: to an authority; sender's address, date, recipient's address, subject line, Dear Sir/Madam, body paragraphs, Yours faithfully, full name
Common punctuation: full stop (.), comma (,), question mark (?), exclamation mark (!), apostrophe (don't = do not), colon (:), semi-colon (;)
Spelling rules: ie vs. ei (believe, receive), double consonant (running, sitting), dropping final e before vowel suffix (love → loving)
Common errors in JSS writing: comma splice, run-on sentences, lack of subject-verb agreement, inconsistent tense
Paragraphing: new idea = new paragraph; indent or skip a line
Sentence variety: short punchy sentences for effect; longer for description; questions to engage reader
activities: Write a 3-paragraph narrative: paragraph 1 (introduce situation), paragraph 2 (event/action), paragraph 3 (resolution/lesson) on 'A day I will never forget'
Write an informal letter to a friend describing your school's last Sports Day
Peer-edit a classmate's letter: check layout, punctuation, paragraph breaks and tone
exam_focus: BECE tests formal/informal letter writing (layout is heavily marked), narrative essay, and correct punctuation
Formal letter: start 'Dear Sir/Madam', close with 'Yours faithfully'; informal: start 'Dear [name]', close with 'Yours sincerely' or 'Your friend'
Trap: mixing formal and informal language in one letter — decide the register and maintain it throughout

topics.topic: Parts of Speech, Tenses and Sentence Construction
learning_objectives: Identify the eight parts of speech with examples
Use tenses correctly in oral and written contexts
Construct grammatically correct sentences
Distinguish between common errors and correct usage
Apply subject-verb agreement rules
content: Eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection
Nouns: proper (Lagos), common (city), abstract (happiness), collective (flock)
Pronouns: personal (I, you, he, she), possessive (my, your), reflexive (myself), demonstrative (this, that)
Verbs: action verbs (run, eat), linking verbs (is, was, seems), auxiliary/helping verbs (have, will, can)
Adjectives: describe nouns; comparative (-er) and superlative (-est) forms
Adverbs: modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs; often end in -ly
Prepositions: in, on, at, by, for, with, under, between, through
Conjunctions: coordinating (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — FANBOYS), subordinating (because, although, when, if)
Simple present tense: habitual/regular actions; Subject + Verb(+s) for 3rd person singular
Simple past tense: completed actions; regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs (go→went, eat→ate, see→saw)
Present continuous: action happening now; Subject + is/are/am + Verb-ing
Subject-verb agreement: singular subject → singular verb; plural subject → plural verb
activities: Underline and label every word in 5 sentences by its part of speech
Change 10 sentences from present to past tense; identify which verbs are regular and which are irregular
Spot the error: teacher provides 10 sentences with one grammatical error each; students find and correct them
exam_focus: BECE tests part of speech identification, tense usage, and subject-verb agreement — practise with real sentences
Know the 25 most common irregular verbs: go/went, have/had, do/did, say/said, get/got, come/came, make/made, etc.
Trap: 'Neither the students nor the teacher ARE here' — verb agrees with the NEARER subject (teacher — singular); should be 'is'

topics.topic: Team Games — Rules, Skills and Tactics
learning_objectives: Demonstrate basic skills in at least two team sports
Apply rules and regulations of team sports correctly
Demonstrate fair play, teamwork and sportsmanship
Identify positions and their roles in team sports
Apply basic offensive and defensive tactics
content: Football (Soccer): field dimensions (100–110 m × 64–75 m), 11 players per side, 90 minutes, offside rule, fouls and free kicks, goal kick, throw-in, corner kick, penalties; basic skills: dribbling, passing, shooting, heading, trapping

Basketball: court (28 m × 15 m), 5 players per side, 4 quarters (10 min each), scoring (1, 2, 3 points), violations (travelling, double dribble, shot clock), basic skills: dribbling, passing (chest, bounce, overhead), shooting, rebounding
Handball: court (40 m × 20 m), 7 players per side, 2 halves (30 min), D-zone, throwing and catching; basic skills: overarm throw, catching, dribbling
Volleyball: 6 players per side, 5 sets (first to 25, 5th to 15), rotations, libero, skills: forearm pass (dig), set, spike, serve, block
Athletics track and field: sprints (100m, 200m, 400m), relays (4×100m, 4×400m), throws (shot put, discus, javelin), jumps (long jump, high jump, triple jump)
Teamwork principles: communication, positioning, covering, interchanging
Fair play: respecting opponents, officials and rules; acknowledging good performance by opponents
Sportsmanship: winning and losing with grace; no arguing with officials; helping injured opponents
activities: Practise the three phases of basketball: dribbling relay, passing drills, free throw shooting competition
Play mini-football (5-a-side) with emphasis on one rule: the offside rule — observe and discuss incidents
Conduct a round-robin volleyball tournament; one team acts as officials, one plays, one observes and records violations
exam_focus: BECE tests: rules of major sports (number of players, duration, scoring, major violations), basic skills identification, and fair play principles
Know: football = 11 players, 90 min; basketball = 5 players, 40 min; volleyball = 6 players; handball = 7 players
Trap: 'offside in football' — the player must be in the opposition's half AND nearer to the goal than the second-to-last defender when the ball is played to them

topics.topic: Personal Hygiene, Nutrition and First Aid
learning_objectives: Explain personal and environmental hygiene practices
Identify the nutrients in food and their functions
Design a balanced diet using local Nigerian foods
Demonstrate basic first aid procedures for common injuries
Explain the dangers of drug abuse
content: Personal hygiene: bathing regularly, hand washing (before eating, after toilet), dental care (brushing twice daily), clean clothing, cutting fingernails
Environmental hygiene: disposal of waste (refuse, sewage), drainage, clean water sources, avoiding open defecation
Water-borne diseases associated with poor hygiene: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, guinea worm

Nutrients: carbohydrates (energy — rice, bread, yam, corn), proteins (growth and repair — meat, beans, eggs, fish), fats (energy and insulation — palm oil, groundnut), vitamins (regulatory — fruits, vegetables), minerals (structural — milk, liver, beans), water
Balanced diet: all nutrients in right proportions; using Nigerian foods: plate model — half vegetables, quarter carbohydrates, quarter protein
Malnutrition: under-nutrition (kwashiorkor — protein deficiency; marasmus — total calorie deficiency) and over-nutrition (obesity)
First aid: immediate assistance given to an injured person before professional medical help
First aid for cuts: clean wound, apply pressure, bandage; for burns: cool with running water for 10 minutes (NOT ice, NOT butter)
First aid for fractures: immobilise (splint), do not move unnecessarily, seek medical help
Nosebleed: lean FORWARD (not back), pinch soft part of nose for 10 minutes
Drug abuse: using drugs for non-medical purposes or in wrong doses; examples: cannabis, tramadol (abuse), alcohol excess, tobacco
Effects of drug abuse: addiction, mental illness, liver disease, HIV risk (sharing needles), broken families
activities: Conduct a personal hygiene checklist survey for the class; identify most and least practised habits; design an improvement plan
Use the Nigerian food composition chart to plan a one-day balanced diet for a 12-year-old using only local foods within ₦500
Demonstrate first aid for a burn injury using the RCOS protocol: Remove from danger, Cool (running water), Cover (clean cloth), Seek medical help
exam_focus: BECE tests personal hygiene practices, food nutrient classification, first aid steps for common injuries, and drug abuse consequences
Know: for burns — COOL with running water for 10 minutes (NOT butter, NOT ice); for nosebleed — lean FORWARD (NOT backward)
Trap: 'marasmus' is total calorie (energy) deficiency; 'kwashiorkor' is specifically PROTEIN deficiency — different nutritional disorders

learning_objectives: Identify the major bones of the human skeleton
Describe the functions of the skeletal system
Classify joints and describe their movements
Identify major muscle groups and their functions in movement
Explain how muscles and bones work together in physical activity
content: Skeletal system: 206 bones in adult; framework for body; protects organs; supports upright posture; enables movement; produces blood cells (red bone marrow); stores calcium
Axial skeleton: skull, vertebral column (33 vertebrae), ribcage (12 pairs of ribs + sternum)
Appendicular skeleton: pectoral girdle + arms (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges); pelvic girdle + legs (femur, tibia, fibula, patella, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges)
Joint types: fixed/immovable (skull sutures); slightly movable (vertebrae, pubic symphysis); freely movable/synovial (hip, knee, shoulder, elbow, wrist, ankle)
Synovial joint structures: articular cartilage, synovial fluid, joint capsule, ligaments
Types of synovial joints: ball-and-socket (hip, shoulder — widest range of motion), hinge (knee, elbow — flexion/extension only), pivot (neck — rotation), saddle (thumb), gliding/plane (carpals)
Muscular system: over 600 muscles; types: skeletal (voluntary, striped — movement), smooth (involuntary — organs), cardiac (heart)

Major muscle groups: quadriceps (front of thigh — extension), hamstrings (back of thigh — flexion), gastrocnemius/calf (plantarflexion), deltoid (shoulder — abduction), biceps (elbow flexion), triceps (elbow extension), core muscles (trunk stability)
Antagonistic muscle pairs: when agonist (prime mover) contracts, antagonist relaxes; biceps/triceps example
Muscle contraction: concentric (shortening), eccentric (lengthening under load), isometric (no change in length)
activities: Label a diagram of the human skeleton with 20 named bones; group them into axial and appendicular
Identify the type of joint at: shoulder, knee, skull, elbow, hip, and vertebral column; justify each classification
Perform bicep curl; identify agonist (biceps), antagonist (triceps), synergist (brachialis), and joint (hinge at elbow)
exam_focus: BECE tests major bone names, joint classification, skeletal functions, and muscle groups involved in common movements
Know the antagonistic pair for major movements: biceps/triceps (elbow), quadriceps/hamstrings (knee)
Trap: ligaments connect bone to bone; tendons connect muscle to bone — a common confusion that BECE tests

learning_objectives: State the seven characteristics of living things
Classify organisms into the five kingdoms
Distinguish between plant and animal cells using diagrams
Describe the functions of major cell organelles
Explain the importance of microorganisms to humans and the environment
content: Characteristics of living things: MRS GREN — Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition

Five kingdoms: Monera (bacteria — no nucleus), Protista (amoeba, euglena — single-celled eukaryotes), Fungi (mushrooms, moulds — decomposers), Plantae (plants — photosynthesis), Animalia (animals — heterotrophs)
Viruses: not classified in any kingdom; non-living outside host; consist of genetic material (DNA or RNA) + protein coat
Cell theory: all organisms are made of cells; cell is basic unit of life; cells arise from existing cells
Animal cell structures: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, Golgi body, lysosomes
Plant cell additional structures: cell wall (cellulose), chloroplast (photosynthesis), large permanent vacuole
Differences: plant cells have cell wall, chloroplasts and permanent vacuole; animal cells do not
Microscope: light microscope in JSS labs; parts — eyepiece, objective lens, stage, mirror/light, coarse and fine focus
Magnification: total magnification = eyepiece lens power × objective lens power
Beneficial microorganisms: decomposition (recycle nutrients), nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium), fermentation (yeast for bread/beer), antibiotics (Penicillium mould)
Harmful microorganisms: disease-causing bacteria (cholera, tuberculosis), viruses (malaria — wrong, it's protozoa; HIV/AIDS)
activities: Prepare and observe onion epidermis and cheek cells under the microscope; draw and label both at ×100 and ×400 magnification
Create a classification key for 10 organisms: is it living? Does it have cells? Does it have a nucleus? Does it photosynthesise?
Investigate fermentation: mix yeast, warm water and sugar in a bottle with a balloon on top; observe CO₂ production over 30 minutes
exam_focus: BECE tests MRS GREN (memorise all 7), plant vs. animal cell differences, kingdom names with examples, and microscope parts
Know: chloroplasts and cell wall are in PLANT cells only; lysosomes are mainly in ANIMAL cells
Trap: malaria is caused by Plasmodium (a PROTOZOAN — kingdom Protista), NOT a bacterium; HIV/AIDS is caused by a VIRUS

learning_objectives: Explain the process of photosynthesis and identify its raw materials and products
Describe the human digestive system and identify organs and their functions
Identify the six food classes, their functions and Nigerian food sources
Identify common nutritional deficiency diseases in Nigeria
Perform food tests to identify nutrients
content: Photosynthesis equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in chloroplasts)
Raw materials: carbon dioxide (from air through stomata), water (from soil through roots), light energy (from sun)
Products: glucose (stored as starch or used for energy) and oxygen (released as by-product)
Leaf adaptations for photosynthesis: broad flat shape (surface area), chlorophyll (absorbs light), stomata (gas exchange), transparent epidermis (light penetration)

Food classes: carbohydrates (energy: rice, yam, bread), proteins (growth: beans, meat, fish, eggs), fats (energy storage: palm oil, avocado), vitamins (regulatory: fruits, leafy vegetables), minerals (structural: milk, beans), water (solvent)
Food tests: iodine → blue-black (starch present); Benedict's → brick red (reducing sugar); Biuret → purple (protein); brown paper → translucent mark (fat)

Human digestive system: mouth (chewing, salivary amylase) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (HCl, pepsin) → small intestine (absorption, bile, pancreatic juice) → large intestine (water absorption) → rectum → anus
Villi: finger-like projections in small intestine; increase surface area; microvilli on villi; glucose and amino acids into blood; fatty acids into lacteal

Nutritional deficiency diseases: kwashiorkor (protein → swollen belly, discoloured hair), marasmus (total calorie → wasting), scurvy (Vitamin C → bleeding gums), rickets (Vitamin D/Ca → bow legs), night blindness (Vitamin A → poor night vision), anaemia (iron → fatigue, pale skin), goitre (iodine → swollen neck)
activities: Test three food samples (bread, milk, vegetable oil) for starch, protein and fat; record observations and conclusions in a results table
Demonstrate the conditions needed for photosynthesis: use a destarched plant, cover one leaf with foil; after 6 hours in light, test both for starch
Match deficiency diseases to their missing nutrient: make a matching game; learn by repetition
exam_focus: BECE consistently tests food tests (know ALL four), deficiency diseases with their nutrients, and photosynthesis equation
Memorise ALL 7 deficiency diseases with their cause, symptom, and food source
Trap: photosynthesis uses CO₂ and produces O₂; respiration uses O₂ and produces CO₂ — they are OPPOSITE processes but both happen in plants

topics.topic: States of Matter, Separation and Changes
learning_objectives: Describe the three states of matter and their properties in terms of particle arrangement
Explain changes of state using particle theory
Distinguish between physical and chemical changes
Describe and explain methods of separating mixtures
Distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures
content: States of matter: solid (fixed shape, fixed volume, particles close together, vibrate in fixed positions), liquid (fixed volume, no fixed shape, particles close but free to move), gas (no fixed shape or volume, particles far apart, move rapidly in all directions)

Changes of state: melting (solid → liquid, absorbs heat), freezing (liquid → solid, releases heat), evaporation (liquid → gas surface, absorbs heat), boiling (liquid → gas throughout, at boiling point), condensation (gas → liquid, releases heat), sublimation (solid → gas directly: e.g. iodine, dry ice)
Physical change: no new substance formed; reversible; change in state, shape or size (e.g. melting ice, dissolving salt)
Chemical change: new substance(s) formed; usually irreversible; change in chemical composition (e.g. burning wood, cooking food, rusting)
Pure substance vs. mixture: pure substance (one type of particle — element or compound); mixture (two or more substances combined, not chemically combined)

Separation of mixtures: filtration (insoluble solid from liquid), evaporation (soluble solid from solution — crystallisation), distillation (liquids with different boiling points), chromatography (coloured substances — different solubility), magnetism (magnetic from non-magnetic), decantation (liquid from settled solid), sieving (different particle sizes)
Elements: substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances; 118 known elements; arranged in periodic table
Compounds: substances formed when two or more elements combine chemically; fixed ratio; different properties from constituent elements (e.g. H₂O is neither hydrogen nor oxygen)
Mixtures: two or more substances physically combined; variable ratio; each retains its own properties (e.g. saltwater)
activities: Set up a filtration experiment to separate sand from salt water; then evaporate the filtrate to recover salt crystals
Investigate paper chromatography using black marker pen ink and water; observe how many colours separate and explain why
Classify 10 household changes as physical or chemical: ironing a shirt, burning wood, mixing salt in water, cooking egg, melting butter — justify each
exam_focus: BECE tests separation method for given mixture type, physical vs. chemical change identification, and states of matter properties
Know WHICH separation method for WHICH mixture type: filtration = insoluble solid + liquid; evaporation = dissolved solid + liquid; distillation = two miscible liquids
Trap: dissolving is a PHYSICAL change (you can evaporate the water to get the salt back); burning is CHEMICAL (you cannot un-burn wood)

learning_objectives: Identify and give examples of the different forms of energy
Explain energy conversion with practical examples
State the law of conservation of energy
Describe the structure of a simple electric circuit
Explain the difference between conductors and insulators
content: Forms of energy: kinetic (moving objects), potential (stored in position — gravitational, elastic), heat/thermal, light, sound, chemical (food, fuel, batteries), electrical, nuclear
Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only change from one form to another

Energy conversions: solar panel (light → electrical), electric motor (electrical → kinetic), generator (kinetic → electrical), battery (chemical → electrical), bulb (electrical → light + heat), car engine (chemical → kinetic + heat)
Electric circuit: closed path through which electricity flows; components: battery/cell (source of EMF), switch (open/close circuit), bulb/resistor (load), wires (conductor)
Series circuit: components connected end to end; same current through all; one break stops the whole circuit
Parallel circuit: components on separate branches; each has same voltage; one branch can be broken without affecting others
Electrical symbols: cell (─┤├─), battery (─┤├┤├─), bulb (─⊗─), switch (─/─), resistor (─▭─), ammeter (─A─), voltmeter (─V─)
Conductors: allow electricity to flow; metals (copper, aluminium, silver, gold); carbon (graphite)
Insulators: do not allow electricity to flow; rubber, plastic, glass, wood, ceramic, dry air
Domestic electrical safety: fuses, circuit breakers, earthing, not overloading sockets, not using damaged wires
Renewable energy in Nigeria: solar power (rural electrification), small hydro, wind; importance for reducing dependence on fossil fuels
activities: Build a simple series circuit with a battery, two bulbs, and a switch; observe what happens when one bulb is removed; rebuild as parallel
Investigate conductors and insulators: use a circuit with a battery, bulb and two wires; test various objects (coin, rubber, pencil, wood, nail, plastic) to see which complete the circuit
Energy conversion poster: draw a chain of energy conversions in a hydroelectric dam from water in reservoir to light in a home
exam_focus: BECE tests energy form identification, energy conversion examples, circuit diagrams (series vs. parallel), and conductor/insulator classification
Know all circuit symbols by drawing — BECE may ask you to draw a circuit
Trap: in a SERIES circuit, removing ONE bulb breaks the whole circuit; in PARALLEL, the other bulbs continue — this is a common BECE question

learning_objectives: Define ecosystem and describe its components
Construct food chains and food webs from given data
Explain the effects of pollution on the environment
Describe conservation measures in Nigeria
Explain the causes and consequences of climate change
content: Ecosystem: a community of living organisms (biotic) interacting with each other and their non-living environment (abiotic) in a specific area
Biotic components: producers (green plants), consumers (animals), decomposers (bacteria and fungi)
Abiotic components: temperature, light, water, soil, wind, minerals
Food chain: shows feeding relationships; arrows show direction of energy flow; e.g. grass → grasshopper → lizard → eagle
Food web: multiple interconnected food chains; more realistic representation of ecosystem feeding
Trophic levels: producers (level 1), primary consumers (level 2), secondary consumers (level 3), tertiary consumers (level 4)
Energy loss: only 10% of energy passed to next level; rest lost as heat, excretion, movement

Pollution: introduction of harmful substances into the environment; types — air (vehicle exhaust, factory smoke), water (oil spill, sewage, chemicals), land/soil (refuse dumps, chemicals, erosion), noise (generators, traffic, construction)
Effects of pollution in Nigeria: oil spills (Niger Delta — Ogoni land devastation), deforestation (loss of biodiversity), flooding (blocked drainage + building on flood plains)
Conservation: protection and wise use of natural resources; National Parks in Nigeria: Yankari (Bauchi), Cross River, Okomu (Edo), Kamuku
Climate change: global warming due to greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide) trapping heat; effects — rising sea levels, erratic rainfall, flooding, drought
Individual actions: reduce, reuse, recycle; planting trees; using energy-saving bulbs; reducing waste
activities: Draw a food web for a savanna ecosystem: grass, acacia tree, zebra, impala, lion, hyena, vulture, termite, fungi; identify the producers and top predator
Investigate pollution in the local environment: survey the school's waste disposal methods; identify pollutants and suggest improvements
Calculate: if grass contains 10,000 J of energy, how much reaches a hawk (4th trophic level) using the 10% rule?
exam_focus: BECE tests food chain construction, energy flow (10% rule), pollution types and their effects, and conservation area examples in Nigeria
Know 3 National Parks in Nigeria by name and state: Yankari (Bauchi), Cross River NP, Kamuku (Kaduna)
Trap: arrows in food chains point FROM the organism eaten TO the organism eating — they show ENERGY FLOW, not 'who eats who'

learning_objectives: Describe types and functions of the family
Explain the importance of community and community development
Demonstrate core social values in daily interactions
Analyse the impact of social values on national development
Evaluate the role of the school in promoting social values
content: Definition of family: the smallest social unit; the basic building block of society

Types of family: nuclear (father, mother, children — most common in cities), extended (includes grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins — more common in rural Nigeria), single-parent, blended (step-family), foster family
Functions of the family: biological (reproduction), economic (provision of needs), socialisation (teaching values and norms), protection (safety, care), psychological (love, belonging)
Community: a group of people living in the same area and sharing common interests or characteristics
Types of community: rural (farming, close-knit, traditional), urban (diverse, industrial, fast-paced), sub-urban (between rural and urban)
Community development: process of improving living conditions through collective action; local government involvement, CBOs (Community-Based Organisations)
Social values: shared beliefs and standards that guide behaviour in society

Core social values in Nigeria: honesty (telling the truth), respect (honouring elders and authority), responsibility (being accountable), tolerance (accepting differences), compassion (caring for others), hard work, patriotism
Cultural values vs. universal values: traditional practices may vary; some values transcend culture (human dignity, justice)
The school as a social institution: transmits values, develops skills, prepares citizens
Agents of socialisation: family (first and most powerful), school, peer group, mass media, religious institutions
activities: Draw a genogram (family tree) showing at least three generations; identify nuclear and extended family members
Class survey: identify one community problem in your neighbourhood (e.g. poor roads, waste disposal) and design a simple community action plan
Values auction: each student receives 10 value tokens; they bid for values listed on cards; at the end, discuss why they chose those values
exam_focus: BECE tests types of family with examples, functions of family, types of community, and list of social values
Know all 5+ functions of the family: biological, economic, socialisation, protection, psychological (emotional)
Trap: a nuclear family is NOT the same as a small family — it specifically refers to ONLY parents and their unmarried children, regardless of size

topics.topic: Three Tiers and Three Arms of Government
learning_objectives: Describe the three tiers of government in Nigeria
Explain the roles of the executive, legislative and judicial arms
Identify Nigerian citizens' rights and responsibilities
Explain the role of INEC in democracy
Demonstrate civic responsibilities in school and community
content: Three tiers of government in Nigeria: Federal (President + National Assembly + Judiciary — Abuja), State (Governor + State House of Assembly — each state capital), Local Government (Chairman + Legislative Council — 774 LGAs)
Federal capital: Abuja; 36 states + FCT; 774 LGAs
Three arms of government: Executive (implements/executes laws), Legislature (makes laws), Judiciary (interprets laws and settles disputes)
Federal Executive: President (Commander-in-Chief + Head of State + Head of Government), Vice President, Ministers, security agencies
National Assembly: Senate (109 senators — 3 per state + 1 FCT) + House of Representatives (360 members); passes bills, approves budget, confirms ministerial appointments
Judiciary: Supreme Court (highest; final appeals), Court of Appeal, Federal High Court, State High Courts; independent of other arms
Separation of powers and checks and balances: prevents any one arm from becoming too powerful
Fundamental Human Rights (Chapter IV, 1999 Constitution): right to life, dignity, freedom from slavery, fair hearing, freedom of thought/expression/religion, right to education
Citizens' responsibilities: obey the law, pay taxes, vote, defend the country, respect others' rights, protect the environment
INEC: conducts elections; registers voters and parties; declares results; maintains election register
Democracy: government of the people, by the people, for the people (Abraham Lincoln)
activities: Create a government structure chart: three arms × three tiers = nine-box grid; fill in the name of the institution in each box
Mock parliament: class creates a bill ('All students must wear uniforms'); debate in two houses; vote; the 'President' assents or withholds
Rights and responsibilities card sort: given 20 cards (half rights, half responsibilities), sort them into two groups; then match each right to a corresponding responsibility
exam_focus: BECE tests the three tiers and arms, functions of each arm, fundamental human rights, and INEC's role
Know the numbers: 109 senators, 360 House reps, 36 states, 774 LGAs
Trap: the JUDICIARY does not make laws (that is the Legislature) — it INTERPRETS and APPLIES the law

topics.topic: Democracy, Electoral Process and Conflict Resolution
learning_objectives: Explain the principles and features of democracy
Describe the electoral process in Nigeria step by step
Apply conflict resolution strategies in school and community
Explain the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC)
Evaluate Nigeria's democratic journey from independence to present
content: Democracy: government based on free and fair elections, majority rule with minority rights, rule of law, separation of powers, freedom of press
Democratic principles: sovereignty of the people, political equality, majority rule, protection of minority rights, civil liberties, accountability of leaders
Nigeria's democratic history: Independence 1960 (parliamentary), 1st Republic 1963 (republican), military (1966), 2nd Republic (1979–1983), military (1983–1999), 4th Republic (1999–present)
Electoral process in Nigeria: voter registration → party primaries → campaign period → polling day (accreditation → voting → counting) → collation → declaration → possible tribunal petition
INEC responsibilities: register voters, register parties, conduct elections, train ad hoc officials, announce results, handle electoral offences
Types of electoral malpractice: underage voting, ballot box snatching, vote buying, result manipulation, voter intimidation
Conflict: a disagreement or clash between opposing groups; types — intrapersonal (within oneself), interpersonal (between individuals), intergroup (between groups), international
Causes of conflict: injustice, inequality, intolerance, resource competition, miscommunication, tribalism, religious differences
Conflict resolution methods: negotiation (direct discussion), mediation (neutral third party), arbitration (binding decision from arbitrator), litigation (courts), compromise
UNCRC (1989): 54 articles protecting children's rights: survival (life, food, water), development (education, play), protection (from abuse, exploitation), participation (express views)
Child rights in Nigeria: Child Rights Act 2003; 28 states have domesticated it; challenges of implementation
activities: Simulate a community conflict: two village groups want the only borehole for different purposes; apply mediation steps to reach a compromise
Research: which year was Nigeria under civilian government vs. military rule? Draw a governance timeline from 1960 to 2023
Write a letter to the INEC Chairman suggesting two reforms to improve Nigeria's electoral process, using evidence from recent elections
exam_focus: BECE tests principles of democracy, electoral process steps, INEC's role, conflict resolution methods, and child rights
Know the 4 categories of UNCRC rights: survival, development, protection, participation
Trap: negotiation is DIRECT (no third party); mediation has a NEUTRAL third party who facilitates; arbitration has a third party whose decision is BINDING

learning_objectives: Identify major environmental challenges facing Nigeria
Explain the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Suggest practical solutions to environmental problems at community level
Evaluate individual and collective responsibility for the environment
Explain the relationship between environment and national development
content: Environmental challenges in Nigeria: deforestation (logging, farming, fuelwood), desertification (northward advance of Sahara Desert), flooding (Lagos, Rivers State), erosion (Anambra, Enugu, Cross River), oil pollution (Niger Delta), solid waste disposal, water pollution
Causes: overpopulation, poverty, poor governance, industrial activities, climate change, poor land use practices
Effects of deforestation: loss of biodiversity, increased soil erosion, reduced rainfall, climate change contribution
Effects of oil pollution (Niger Delta): destruction of fishing grounds, contamination of drinking water, health problems, displacement of communities
UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 17 goals adopted by 193 UN member states in 2015; achieve by 2030

Key SDGs relevant to Nigeria: SDG 1 (No poverty), SDG 2 (Zero hunger), SDG 3 (Good health), SDG 4 (Quality education), SDG 6 (Clean water and sanitation), SDG 7 (Affordable clean energy), SDG 11 (Sustainable cities), SDG 13 (Climate action), SDG 15 (Life on land), SDG 16 (Peace and justice)
Nigeria's SDG progress: mixed performance; education improvements (but still high out-of-school children), health challenges (malaria, maternal mortality), economic inequality
Individual actions: recycling, saving water and energy, planting trees, reducing plastic use, proper waste disposal
Collective actions: community clean-up, reforestation programmes, advocacy, policy reform campaigns
activities: Create a visual poster on one SDG that Nigeria is struggling with; include statistics, causes, and 3 achievable solutions
Conduct a school environmental audit: assess waste disposal, water use, energy use; present findings to school management
Debate: 'Economic development in Nigeria is incompatible with environmental protection' — support or oppose with evidence
exam_focus: BECE tests major environmental problems in Nigeria, their causes and effects, and at least 5 SDGs by number and name
Know which states/regions are associated with each problem: Niger Delta (oil pollution), Anambra/Enugu (erosion), Northern states (desertification), Lagos (flooding, waste)
Trap: SDGs were adopted in 2015 (NOT 2000 — that was MDGs, the Millennium Development Goals) with a target of 2030

learning_objectives: Define business and explain why people engage in business
Distinguish between industry, commerce and services
Identify entrepreneurial characteristics and opportunities
Explain the importance of small businesses to the Nigerian economy
Identify career opportunities in business
content: Business: any activity carried out to produce goods or services to satisfy human needs and make profit

Types of business activities: production/industry (extractive — mining, farming; manufacturing — turning raw materials into goods; construction — building), commerce (trade + aids to trade), services (direct services — doctors, teachers, lawyers; commercial services — transport, banking, insurance)
The business cycle: production → distribution → consumption
Needs vs. wants: needs are essential (food, shelter, clothing); wants are desirable (TV, car, luxury goods)
Entrepreneur: person who identifies a business opportunity, takes risks to organise resources and manage a business for profit
Characteristics of an entrepreneur: initiative, risk-taking, creativity, determination, leadership, problem-solving, self-confidence
Entrepreneurship opportunities in Nigeria: agribusiness, ICT services, fashion/tailoring, food processing, transport, e-commerce
SMEs (Small and Medium Enterprises): backbone of Nigerian economy; major employer; SMEDAN, BOI (Bank of Industry) support SMEs
Business ownership types at JSS level: sole proprietorship, partnership, cooperative
Importance of business to national development: employment creation, tax revenue, innovation, import substitution
activities: Identify a business problem in your school: e.g. lack of affordable stationery; design a simple business idea to solve it; present to class
Interview a local small business owner (market trader, artisan, etc.): find out how they started, their challenges, and their advice
Class entrepreneurship fair: each student brings one product made from local materials; display and present their 'business'
exam_focus: BECE tests industry classification (extractive, manufacturing, construction), distinction between industry and commerce, and entrepreneur characteristics
Know examples of each industry type: extractive (coal mining, cassava farming), manufacturing (Nasco biscuits, Dangote cement), construction (Julius Berger roads)
Trap: banks, insurance and transport are AIDS TO TRADE (part of commerce) — not industries — though transport companies may engage in industry

learning_objectives: Describe the functions and organisation of a business office
Identify office equipment and their uses
Apply business communication skills (memos, letters, reports, emails)
Demonstrate basic keyboarding techniques using the home row method
Explain filing and record management systems
content: Office: the nerve centre of a business; where information is collected, processed, stored and distributed
Functions of an office: receiving information, recording information, organising information, distributing information, safeguarding assets (filing and custody)
Types of offices: open plan (no partitions — good for teamwork), private (individual cubicles — good for confidential work), virtual (remote, no physical location)
Office equipment: typewriter/computer, photocopier, printer, scanner, shredder, telephone, filing cabinet, fax machine
Business communication types: internal (within organisation — memo, circular, notice board, email) and external (outside — business letter, report, fax, email)
Memo (memorandum): internal document; TO, FROM, DATE, SUBJECT headings; formal but internal
Business letter: external; sender's address, date, recipient's address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close, signature
Report: structured document presenting findings; headings — Title, Introduction, Findings, Recommendations, Conclusion
Keyboarding: QWERTY keyboard; home row keys (ASDF JKL;); correct finger placement; posture (straight back, feet flat); aim for speed and accuracy
Touch typing: typing without looking at keyboard; increases speed and efficiency
Filing systems: alphabetical (by name), numerical (by number), geographical (by location), chronological (by date), subject (by topic)
Record management: creating, maintaining, protecting, storing and disposing of records systematically
activities: Write a memo from the school principal to all teachers about a change in assembly time; follow correct memo format
Practise home row keyboarding: ASDF JKL; for 10 minutes daily; track words per minute over a week
Set up a simple filing system for the class register using alphabetical order; practice retrieving a file by name
exam_focus: BECE tests office functions, internal vs. external communication types, memo vs. business letter format, and filing system names
Memo format: TO: / FROM: / DATE: / SUBJECT: — no 'Dear' or 'Yours faithfully'
Trap: a memo is INTERNAL (within the organisation); a business letter is EXTERNAL (to outside parties) — they have different formats

topics.topic: Introduction to Bookkeeping and Basic Accounts
learning_objectives: Define bookkeeping and distinguish it from accounting
Apply the double-entry principle to basic transactions
Record transactions in a simple cash book
Prepare a simple income and expenditure statement
Understand the importance of record-keeping for small businesses
content: Bookkeeping: systematic recording of financial transactions of a business; quantitative, routine task
Accounting: broader concept; includes bookkeeping + interpretation + analysis + reporting
Why records matter: know profit/loss, track debtors/creditors, meet tax obligations, plan the business, access loans
Source documents: receipt (proof of payment), invoice (bill for goods), delivery note, bank statement
Accounting equation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities; business is separate from owner (entity concept)
Assets: things owned by the business (cash, stock, equipment, building, debtors)
Liabilities: amounts owed by the business (creditors, loans, bank overdraft)
Capital: amount invested by owner; owner's equity
Double-entry: every transaction has two effects — one account debited, another credited; total debits = total credits
Simple cash book: records all cash received (receipts — left/debit side) and cash paid out (payments — right/credit side); balance = closing cash
Simple income statement: Income − Expenses = Profit (or Loss); used for small businesses and petty traders
Ledger accounts (T-accounts): Dr side (debit) on left; Cr side (credit) on right; balanced at end of period
activities: Record a week of a small suya seller's transactions in a simple cash book; balance the book; identify closing cash
Given: Cash ₦50,000; Debtors ₦20,000; Goods ₦30,000; Loan ₦40,000; calculate Capital using the accounting equation
Categorise 15 items as assets, liabilities or capital: motor vehicle, bank loan, cash in till, merchandise, creditors, building, overdraft, equipment
exam_focus: BECE tests accounting equation, asset/liability/capital classification, simple cash book balancing, and bookkeeping vs. accounting distinction
The accounting equation is the foundation: A = C + L; if two values are given, you can always find the third
Trap: capital is NOT the same as profit — capital is what the owner put in; profit is what was earned from trading

learning_objectives: Describe the major pre-colonial Nigerian states and their organization
Explain the economic, political and social structures of pre-colonial societies
Trace major trade routes and trade activities in pre-colonial Nigeria
Identify the cultural achievements of pre-colonial Nigerian civilizations
Explain the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade and its impact on Nigeria
content: Nok Culture (500 BC–AD 200): earliest known civilisation in Nigeria; iron technology; famous terracotta sculptures found in Plateau State
Oyo Empire (14th–19th century): Yoruba; powerful cavalry-based military; Alaafin as ruler; Oyo Mesi (council of chiefs) as checks on Alaafin; extensive trade network

Benin Kingdom (12th century–1897): Bini/Edo; the Oba as divine ruler; renowned bronze and ivory art (Benin Bronzes — now disputed in British Museum); strong military; destroyed by British Punitive Expedition 1897

Hausa States (Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir, etc.): northern Nigeria; independent city-states; trade centres; Islam introduced in 14th century; conquered by Fulani jihad (Usman dan Fodio 1804) → Sokoto Caliphate
Sokoto Caliphate (1804): Usman dan Fodio launched jihad to reform Islam; created largest empire in 19th century Africa; Emirs as local rulers; still influential today
Igbo societies: decentralised (no single king); governed by age grades, title societies (Ozo), oracle systems (Chukwu oracle); Arochukwu Confederacy important in slave trade
Tiv, Idoma, Ijaw, Efik and other communities: diverse structures; Efik of Calabar dominant in coastal trade

Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade (16th–19th century): approximately 3.5 million Nigerians enslaved; Badagry and Calabar as major ports; consequences — depopulation, economic disruption, warfare between communities, psychological trauma
Legitimate trade: after abolition, shift to palm oil, cotton, groundnut, timber; 'Oil Rivers' in the Delta
activities: Draw a map of Nigeria marking the locations of the major pre-colonial states and kingdoms studied
Research: what happened to the Benin Bronzes? Write a 200-word letter from Nigeria's government to the British Museum requesting their return
Timeline activity: arrange 10 key pre-colonial events in chronological order from Nok Culture to the Sokoto Caliphate
exam_focus: BECE tests names of major states, their locations, rulers' titles (Alaafin — Oyo; Oba — Benin; Emir — Hausa/Fulani), and the Trans-Atlantic slave trade impact
Know: Oyo = Yoruba; Benin = Bini/Edo (NOT Benin Republic country); Sokoto = Fulani/Hausa; Arochukwu = Igbo
Trap: the Benin Kingdom is in present-day Edo State, Nigeria — NOT the same as the Republic of Benin (country)

learning_objectives: Describe how Britain colonised Nigeria
Explain the amalgamation of Nigeria in 1914
Identify major nationalist leaders and their contributions
Describe the political parties and movements that led to independence
Explain how Nigeria gained independence on October 1, 1960
content: British colonialism: began in earnest with 1861 annexation of Lagos; conquest of Yorubaland (1893), Niger Delta (1880s–1900), Benin Kingdom (1897 Punitive Expedition), Hausa-Fulani states (1903 — Kano and Sokoto), Igbo territory (various campaigns 1900–1920s)
Royal Niger Company (1879–1900): trading company given royal charter to govern the region; surrendered charter 1900
1900: Northern and Southern Protectorates established under direct Crown control

Amalgamation (1914): Governor-General Lord Lugard merged Northern and Southern Nigeria into 'Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria' — January 1, 1914; administered as one entity for administrative efficiency; many Nigerians argue it was a 'marriage of inconvenience'
Indirect rule: Lugard's method of governance — using existing traditional rulers as local administrators; worked in North (Emirs); less successful in East (no chiefs) and West
Nigerian nationalist movement: educated Nigerians and traditional rulers resisting colonial exploitation
Newspapers: Lagos Weekly Record, West African Pilot (Azikiwe) — important tools of nationalism
NCNC (1944): National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons; founded by Herbert Macaulay and Nnamdi Azikiwe; pan-Nigerian
AG (1950): Action Group; founded by Obafemi Awolowo; Yoruba-based
NPC (1949): Northern Peoples' Congress; Ahmadu Bello; Northern-based
Constitutional developments: Macpherson Constitution (1951), Lyttleton Constitution (1954 — federal structure), Independence Constitution (1960)
Independence: October 1, 1960; Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as Prime Minister; Nnamdi Azikiwe as Governor-General (later President of Republic 1963)
activities: Roleplay: an 1885 Berlin Conference where European powers divided Africa — students represent Britain, France, Germany, Belgium; discuss how Nigeria's borders were drawn
Make a 'Father of Nigeria' profile card for: Macaulay, Azikiwe, Awolowo, Ahmadu Bello, and Tafawa Balewa — include birth year, state/ethnic group, party, and one achievement
Debate: 'Amalgamation of 1914 was a mistake' — was it good or bad for Nigeria? Use historical evidence
exam_focus: BECE tests: amalgamation date (1914), Lord Lugard, party founders (NCNC–Azikiwe/Macaulay, AG–Awolowo, NPC–Ahmadu Bello), and Independence date (1st October 1960)
Know: PM at Independence = Tafawa Balewa; Governor-General = Azikiwe
Trap: Herbert Macaulay founded the first political party (NNDP 1923) AND co-founded NCNC 1944 — he is called the 'Father of Nigerian Nationalism'

topics.topic: Nigerian History from Independence to the Present
learning_objectives: Trace major events in Nigerian political history from 1960 to present
Explain the causes and consequences of the Nigerian Civil War
Identify major military leaders and their contributions/controversies
Describe Nigeria's return to democracy in 1999
Evaluate the achievements and challenges of Nigerian democracy
content: 1st Republic (1960–1966): parliamentary democracy; PM Tafawa Balewa; 1963 Republican Constitution; three regions; challenges: election crisis 1964, Western Region crisis 1965
January 15, 1966 coup: first military coup by Kaduna Nzeogwu and others; killed many northern leaders and PM Balewa; General Aguiyi-Ironsi became head of state
July 1966 counter-coup: northern officers killed Ironsi; General Yakubu Gowon became Head of State

Civil War (1967–1970): Eastern Region declared Republic of Biafra on May 30, 1967 (Lt. Col. Odumegwu Ojukwu); Federal Government offensive; No-Victor-No-Vanquished policy; ended January 15, 1970; estimated 1–3 million deaths (many from starvation)
Gowon era (1966–1975): created 12 states (1967), 19 states (1976); oil boom ('petrodollars'); ECOWAS founded 1975; ousted in bloodless coup while at OAU summit
Murtala Muhammed (1975–1976): decisive reforms; capital transfer to Abuja announced; assassinated February 13, 1976 by Lt. Col. Dimka
Obasanjo 1 (1976–1979): handed over to civilians; 19 states; transition to 2nd Republic
2nd Republic (1979–1983): presidential system; President Shehu Shagari (NPN); ended in military coup December 31, 1983 citing corruption
Buhari/Idiagbon (1983–1985): WAI (War Against Indiscipline); Decree 4 restricted press freedom; overthrown by Babangida
Babangida era (1985–1993): SAP (Structural Adjustment Programme); June 12 1993 election (MKO Abiola won but annulled); transition to 4th Republic; stepped aside August 1993
Abacha (1993–1998): most brutal military rule; imprisoned opposition; Abiola died in custody 1998; Abacha died June 8, 1998
Abubakar (1998–1999): managed transition to civilian rule; Obasanjo won 1999 election
4th Republic (1999–present): longest unbroken democratic period; Obasanjo (1999–2007), Yar'Adua (2007–2010), Jonathan (2010–2015), Buhari 2 (2015–2023), Tinubu (2023–present)
activities: Create a Nigerian political timeline poster: list every head of state/government from 1960 to present with their years, party/branch (civilian/military), and one key action
Case study: read accounts of the Nigerian Civil War from different perspectives (Federal, Biafran); identify common ground and differences; write a reflective essay
Current affairs: analyse one major challenge facing Nigeria's democracy today (insecurity, corruption, electoral malpractice); suggest constitutional solutions
exam_focus: BECE tests major coup dates, heads of state names, Civil War facts (1967–1970, Ojukwu, Gowon, Biafra), and 1999 return to democracy
Know the order: Balewa → Ironsi → Gowon → Murtala → Obasanjo 1 → Shagari → Buhari 1 → Babangida → Abacha → Abubakar → Obasanjo 2
Trap: the Civil War ended in 1970 with Gowon's 'No Victor, No Vanquished' speech — it is NOT still ongoing

topics.topic: Computer Fundamentals — History, Types and Components
learning_objectives: Define a computer and explain its main functions
Trace the historical development of computers through the generations
Classify computers by size/purpose and by mode of operation
Identify and describe hardware components of a computer
Distinguish between system software and application software
content: Computer: an electronic device that accepts input data, processes it according to instructions (program), stores results, and outputs information
Computer characteristics: speed (billions of operations/second), accuracy (if input is correct, output is correct), reliability (consistent), storage (large memory), diligence (works tirelessly)

Generations of computers: 1st (vacuum tubes — ENIAC 1946), 2nd (transistors — 1950s–60s), 3rd (integrated circuits — 1960s–70s), 4th (microprocessors — 1971–present), 5th (AI and parallel processing — emerging)

Classification by size: supercomputer (weather forecasting, nuclear simulations), mainframe (banks, airlines), minicomputer (medium businesses), microcomputer/personal computer (desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone)
Classification by purpose: general purpose (performs many tasks) vs. special purpose (one specific task — ATM, car engine controller)
Classification by operation: digital (processes binary data — 0s and 1s), analog (processes continuous signals — thermometer), hybrid (both)

Hardware: physical components; input devices (keyboard, mouse, microphone, scanner, webcam, joystick), output devices (monitor, printer, speaker, projector), storage devices (HDD, SSD, USB drive, DVD), processing unit (CPU)
CPU (Central Processing Unit): brain of the computer; Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU — calculations), Control Unit (CU — manages operations), Registers (temporary storage)
Memory: RAM (Random Access Memory — volatile, temporary, working memory), ROM (Read-Only Memory — non-volatile, stores BIOS/firmware)
System software: operates and manages computer hardware; Operating System (Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android, iOS)
Application software: performs specific tasks for users; word processor, spreadsheet, web browser, games, educational software
GIGO: Garbage In, Garbage Out — quality of output depends on quality of input
activities: Label a diagram of a desktop computer: monitor, keyboard, mouse, CPU tower, speakers, printer; classify each as input or output or processing
Create a generations timeline: draw computer shapes for each generation with the technology used and an example from Nigeria's context
Classify 10 software programs as system or application: Windows 10, MS Word, Chrome browser, Android, Photoshop, Ubuntu, WhatsApp, antivirus software
exam_focus: BECE tests computer definition, classification by size/purpose/operation, input/output device identification, and RAM vs. ROM difference
Know: RAM is temporary (lost when power off); ROM is permanent (BIOS stored there); Hard disk is secondary storage (not RAM)
Trap: the keyboard is an INPUT device and the monitor is an OUTPUT device — students sometimes reverse these; a printer is output, not input

topics.topic: Internet, Email, Social Media and Digital Safety
learning_objectives: Explain how the internet works and identify key internet terms
Use email effectively for communication
Identify the benefits and risks of social media
Apply digital safety practices to protect personal information
Describe cyberbullying and explain how to respond to it
content: Internet: global network of computers connected to share information using TCP/IP protocols; not owned by any single entity
World Wide Web (WWW): collection of websites and web pages accessible via the internet; invented by Tim Berners-Lee (1991)

Key internet terms: URL (Uniform Resource Locator — web address), HTTP/HTTPS (protocol for web pages; S = secure), IP address (numerical label for each device), domain name (.com, .ng, .org, .edu), ISP (Internet Service Provider — MTN, Airtel, Glo, 9mobile in Nigeria)
Email: electronic mail; send/receive messages over the internet; faster and cheaper than postal mail
Email structure: From, To, CC (carbon copy), BCC (blind carbon copy), Subject, Body, Attachment
Email etiquette: clear subject line, greeting, concise body, proper closing, professional language in formal email
Social media: websites and apps for creating and sharing content and networking; Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, TikTok, WhatsApp, Telegram
Benefits of social media: communication, education, business, entertainment, activism, information sharing
Risks of social media: cyberbullying, fake news, privacy violation, addiction, screen time, exposure to inappropriate content
Digital safety/cybersecurity: protecting personal information and devices online

Digital safety practices: strong passwords (12+ characters, mix of letters/numbers/symbols), never share passwords, privacy settings, avoid unknown links (phishing), update software, use VPN on public WiFi
Cyberbullying: bullying using digital technology (harassment, spreading rumours, exclusion online); effects on mental health; report to an adult/school authority/platform
Digital footprint: trail of data left when using internet; permanent; potential employers can see it — think before posting
activities: Compose a formal email to a school principal requesting permission for a class excursion; apply correct email format and etiquette
Create a 'Digital Safety Pledge' for the class: list 5 rules everyone agrees to follow online; design as a poster for the ICT lab
Case study: read a scenario of cyberbullying; identify what happened, the impact on the victim, and 4 steps the victim and school should take
exam_focus: BECE tests internet terminology (URL, HTTP, ISP, IP address), email format, social media risks, and digital safety practices
Know: WWW ≠ Internet; internet is the global network infrastructure; WWW is the collection of websites that run ON the internet
Trap: BCC (blind carbon copy) recipients are hidden from other recipients; CC recipients are visible to all — important for professional email

learning_objectives: Identify the key features of a word processing application
Create, format and save a document
Apply text formatting (font, size, bold, italic, underline, alignment, spacing)
Insert tables, images and headers/footers into a document
Use spell check and grammar tools effectively
content: Word processor: software for creating, editing, formatting and printing text documents; examples — Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer
Word processor interface: title bar, menu bar/ribbon (Home, Insert, Layout, Review, View), document area, status bar, scroll bar
Creating a document: File → New; name and save: File → Save As (choose folder and file name); save regularly (Ctrl+S)
Font formatting: font type (Arial, Times New Roman, Calibri), font size (measured in points), font style (bold — Ctrl+B, italic — Ctrl+I, underline — Ctrl+U)
Paragraph alignment: Left (Ctrl+L), Center (Ctrl+E), Right (Ctrl+R), Justify (Ctrl+J)
Line spacing: single, 1.5, double; paragraph spacing (before/after)
Page layout: margins, orientation (portrait/landscape), paper size (A4 most common)
Inserting objects: table (rows and columns for organizing data), image/picture (Insert → Picture), shapes, headers and footers
Header: text appearing at top of every page (e.g. document title); footer: at bottom (e.g. page number)
Cut (Ctrl+X), Copy (Ctrl+C), Paste (Ctrl+V): for moving/duplicating text
Find and Replace (Ctrl+H): replaces specific text throughout document
Spell check and grammar: red wavy underline = spelling error; green = grammar error; right-click for suggestions
activities: Type a 200-word personal essay about yourself in Word/Google Docs; format with 12pt Times New Roman, double spacing, justified alignment, your name as a header
Create a 3-column, 5-row table in Word listing 5 Nigerian states: state name, capital city, major language
Find and replace all occurrences of 'colour' with 'color' in a document; discuss when this might be useful
exam_focus: BECE tests word processor interface components, keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+S = save, Ctrl+B = bold, Ctrl+Z = undo), formatting options, and difference between cut and copy
Know all basic shortcuts: Ctrl+C (copy), Ctrl+X (cut), Ctrl+V (paste), Ctrl+Z (undo), Ctrl+Y (redo), Ctrl+A (select all)
Trap: saving (Ctrl+S) saves to the same location with the same name; Save As (Ctrl+Shift+S or F12) lets you choose new name/location — use Save As for a new document

topics.topic: Spreadsheets (Microsoft Excel / Google Sheets) and Presentations
learning_objectives: Explain the purpose of a spreadsheet application
Enter data and simple formulas into a spreadsheet
Create a basic chart from spreadsheet data
Describe the key features of presentation software
Create a simple presentation with multiple slides
content: Spreadsheet: software for organising, analysing and visualising data in rows and columns; examples — Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets

Spreadsheet interface: cells (intersection of row and column — named by column letter + row number, e.g. A1), rows (horizontal, numbered), columns (vertical, lettered), worksheets (tabs at bottom), workbook (whole file)
Entering data: click cell → type → press Enter (moves down) or Tab (moves right)
Cell references: relative (A1 — changes when copied), absolute ($A$1 — stays fixed when copied)
Formulas: begin with = sign; e.g. =A1+A2, =SUM(A1:A10), =AVERAGE(B2:B6), =MAX(C1:C5), =MIN(C1:C5), =COUNT(D1:D10)
Formatting: number formats (currency ₦, percentage %, date), bold/colour for headers, borders
Charts: select data → Insert → Chart; types — column/bar (comparing categories), line (trends over time), pie (parts of whole)
Presentation software: for creating slideshows; Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, Canva
PowerPoint interface: slide panel (left), slide area (centre), notes panel (bottom), ribbon
Slide layout: title slide, content slide, two-content, blank; choose appropriate layout
Animations and transitions: use sparingly; avoid distraction; must serve the presentation
Design principles for presentations: max 6 words per line, max 6 lines per slide, large readable font (24pt minimum), consistent theme, relevant visuals
activities: Create a spreadsheet of 10 students' test scores in 3 subjects; use SUM and AVERAGE formulas to calculate totals and averages; rank the students
Build a bar chart from the test score spreadsheet; give it a title, label the axes, and choose appropriate colours
Create a 5-slide PowerPoint presentation on 'Water pollution in Nigeria' — include a title slide, 3 content slides (causes, effects, solutions) and a conclusion
exam_focus: BECE tests spreadsheet terminology (cell, row, column, formula), basic functions (SUM, AVERAGE), chart type selection, and presentation design principles
Always start a formula with = in Excel/Sheets; =SUM(A1:A5) adds cells A1 through A5
Trap: cell A1 is column A, row 1 — NOT row A, column 1; remember columns are LETTERS (vertical), rows are NUMBERS (horizontal)

topics.topic: Problem Solving, Algorithms and Introduction to Programming
learning_objectives: Explain what an algorithm is and write simple algorithms
Represent algorithms using flowcharts and pseudocode
Identify input, process and output in a computational problem
Write and run simple code in Scratch or Python
Apply computational thinking (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms) to solve problems
content: Algorithm: a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem; must be clear, finite, and produce a correct result
Characteristics of a good algorithm: clear (unambiguous), ordered (correct sequence), finite (has an endpoint), effective (achieves goal)
Example algorithm — making a phone call: Pick up phone → Unlock screen → Open contacts or dial pad → Enter number → Press call → Wait for response → Speak → End call
Flowchart symbols: Oval/rounded rectangle (Start/End — terminal), Rectangle (Process/action), Diamond (Decision — Yes/No branches), Parallelogram (Input/Output), Arrow (Flow direction)
Pseudocode: structured English-like language describing an algorithm; not real code; readable by humans

Computational thinking components: Decomposition (break problem into smaller parts), Pattern recognition (identify similarities), Abstraction (focus on essential details, ignore irrelevant), Algorithms (step-by-step solution)
Programming: writing instructions for a computer in a programming language
Scratch (MIT): visual block-based programming; good for beginners; drag and drop code blocks; animations, games, stories
Python (basic): text-based language; print() to output; input() to get data; variables to store data; if/else for decisions; for/while loops
Basic Python: print('Hello, World!'); name = input('Enter your name: '); print('Hello, ' + name)
Variables: named storage locations for data; in Python: age = 15; name = 'Fatima'; score = 95.5
Conditional statements (if/else): make decisions; if score >= 50: print('Pass') else: print('Fail')
Loops: repeat actions; for i in range(5): print(i) — prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
activities: Write an algorithm and draw a flowchart for: 'A student wants to determine whether they have passed or failed their exam (pass mark = 50)'
Create a Scratch animation: a cat that moves across the screen, changes colour when clicked, and says 'Hello!' when it reaches the edge
Write a Python program that asks a user for their name and age, then prints a personalised message: 'Hello [name], you are [age] years old'
exam_focus: BECE tests flowchart symbols (oval, rectangle, diamond, parallelogram), algorithm writing, and computational thinking terminology
Know all four flowchart shapes and what each represents — a diagram question WILL appear in BECE
Trap: the diamond in a flowchart represents a DECISION (Yes/No question) — it does NOT represent a process; a rectangle is for processes
